news.title: Trump's Approval Rating in Senate Battlegrounds 2 Weeks Before Midterms
news.text: President Donald Trump’s approval rating remains low in Senate battlegrounds as Democrats and Republicans are engaged in a tight battle for control the upper chamber of Congress just two weeks before the midterm elections. Republicans are facing headwinds as they defend their majority, where they currently hold 53 seats to the Democrats’ 47. Trump’s approval rating, as well as voters’ views about the economy, have fueled a challenging national environment for the GOP two years after Trump’s victory in 2024. Why Trump’s Approval Rating Matters for the Midterms Historically, when the president is unpopular, his party loses seats in the midterms, and Democrats have been favored to retake the House this year. But the Senate has long been seen as a heavier lift. The Maine and North Carolina Senate seats were seen as clear pickups, but no other Republican-held seats were up for grabs in states Trump won by a single-digit margin or lost in 2024. As Trump’s approval rating has fallen, the Senate map has expanded for Democrats. The Cook Political Report lists seven races—Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas—as toss-ups. Trump’s approval rating is underwater in all of those states, according to Civiqs, which has tracked it in every state since the start of second term in January 2025. Whether or not those numbers improve over the next two weeks could play a role in the outcome of those races. Presidential approval is “one of the largest factors [if not the largest factor] driving voter behavior in a midterm election,” Jacob Neiheisel, political science professor at the University at Buffalo, told Newsweek. Neiheisel said he believes Trump’s poor approval numbers has given Democrats the ability to compete in tougher states. “In ‘wave’ elections, the out-party can play on the in-party's side of the field and win rates even in what are, from all outward appearances, safe seats are lower in such years,” he said. Many of those races appear to be close, he said, noting that “a good night for Democrats could mean walking away with quite a few of the toss-up Senate seats.” Whether or not the polls are off, however, will not be known until Election Day, he said. “They have been in recent presidential contests but have been pretty good in midterm races," he said. "There is always a chance, however, that they are missing something.” What Is Donald Trump’s Approval Rating? Trump’s approval ratings have created a headache for Republicans in the final stretch of the campaign, as candidates are making their final pitches to voters. A recent poll from Reuters and Ipsos revealed where Trump’s approval stood nationally. It found that his net approval rating was at -35 points, 31 percent approving and 66 percent disapproving, among 1,679 adults October 16-19, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.4 percentage points. Trump has criticized such polls. On August 30, he posted on Truth Social: “THE FAKE POLLS USED BY OUR CROOKED MEDIA ARE OUT OF CONTROL, AND SOMETHING MUST BE DONE ABOUT IT. FCC TO THE RESCUE! President DJT.” While Democrats believe they may be able to flip the Senate, there is always the possibility of a polling error that could benefit Republicans. In recent cycles, polling has not always been accurate. Republicans have at times overperformed polling averages in key races. Polling errors are not necessarily repeated from cycle to cycle, but a similar error this cycle would not bode well for Democrats’ chances of flipping the Senate. Here is a look at where Trump’s approval rating stands in key races, according to Civiqs. Alaska Although Trump won Alaska by about 13 points in 2024, his approval rating was -12 points—52 percent to 40 percent—in the latest numbers from Civiqs. Alaska has become less solidly conservative over the past few decades. As Democrats gain ground in cities like Anchorage and Fairbanks, Republicans’ statewide margins have narrowed from 31 points in 2000 to about 13 points in 2024 in presidential elections. GOP Senator Dan Sullivan is facing a challenge from former Representative Mary Peltola, the Democrat who represented the state's at-large district from 2022 to 2025. The latest polls show a close race. Peltola led by 2 points, 50 percent to 48 percent, in a survey from InsiderAdvantage conducted October 9-10 with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. A survey from The New York Times and Siena University showed Peltola up 7 points, 50 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 504 likely voters September 24-October 1, with a margin of error of plus or minus 5.1 percentage points. Trump recently campaigned in Alaska, and Sullivan has been supportive of the president. In an October 13 post to Truth Social, Trump described Sullivan as “one of the best and most respected” senators. Sullivan praised Trump in an October 13 post on X: “President Trump is the first president EVER to visit the Mat-Su Valley. If we turn out the Valley, then we turn out Alaska. And if we win Alaska, then we win America.” Iowa Trump’s approval rating in Iowa was -22 points, according to Civiqs, despite him winning the state by around 13 points in 2024. Thirty-four percent of Iowans approve of Trump, while 56 percent disapprove, according to the poll. Iowa was a battleground, backing President Barack Obama in 2008 and 2012, before shifting rightward over the past decade, voting for Trump in all three of his presidential runs. Trump has become a major issue in the race between Republican Representative Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Representative Josh Turek. In Iowa, farmers stand to face impacts from Trump's tariffs and high diesel prices, as agriculture is a key part of the state’s economy. Turek was up 47 percent to 46 percent in a recent YouGov poll of 2,245 likely voters conducted October 6-12. However, an Emerson College poll showed Hinson with a 2-point lead, 47 percent to 45 percent, among 650 likely voters October 5-6. The YouGov poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points, while Emerson's was 3.8. Hinson has walked a fine line on Trump and has put some distance between herself and the president on the issue of the Iran war. “Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran. We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices,” she wrote on September 21 on X. Trump has endorsed Hinson and is expected to visit Iowa. Kansas The Kansas race has become closer than initially expected. GOP Senator Roger Marshall has faced a series of close polls against Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton, and Trump has campaigned in Kansas to give Marshall a boost. Kansans were more split on Trump, with 46 percent disapproving and 45 percent approving, according to Civiqs. Trump won Kansas by about 16 points against former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024. Marshall led Hamilton 48 percent to 47 percent in the latest InsiderAdvantage poll of 1,200 likely voters October 13-14. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. Meanwhile, Hamilton held a 3-point lead in a YouGov poll of 2,253 likely voters September 24-October 4, with 48 percent support to the Republican’s 45 percent. The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.2 percentage points. Marshall has touted his support from Trump, with his campaign previously telling Newsweek that he is a “president who is second to none at getting out the vote.” Maine In Maine, Senator Susan Collins is the only Republican running for reelection in a state that Trump lost in 2024, and she is facing difficult headwinds. Still, she has been able to make a close race due to her personal popularity and moderate image. She faces Democrat Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate. Harris won Maine by 7 points in 2024. Two years later, Trump is 33 points underwater there, according to Civiqs. Only 30 percent of Mainers approve of Trump, while 63 percent disapprove. Collins has never been a particularly close Trump ally and has touted her record on breaking with Trump, such as voting down the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and some Cabinet nominees like Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. However, Democrats have argued that she votes against him when her vote does not tip the scales. During a recent debate, Collins said she is “not exactly his favorite senator” when asked about whether Trump plans to visit Maine before the November 3 election. Collins’ reelection largely rests on her ability to win over ticket-splitters who backed Harris in 2024. A Suffolk University poll gave Jackson a 2-point lead, 49 percent to 47 percent. It surveyed 500 Maine voters October 8-11 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. Jackson was up 4 points among 800 likely voters in a poll from The Washington Post and George Mason University, conducted September 30-October 5. Fifty percent said they planned to vote for Jackson, while 46 percent intended to back Collins. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. Michigan Michigan is the only Democratic-held Senate seat in the toss-up column. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican former Representative Mike Rogers are running to succeed retiring Democrat Gary Peters in a swing state Trump narrowly won in 2024. Trump is now less popular in Michigan, with 33 percent of voters approving of him and 61 percent disapproving, according to Civiqs. Democrats have hoped that the national environment would benefit them in swing states like Michigan, but polls have suggested the race is close. Republicans hope to cast El-Sayed, a progressive endorsed by independent Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, as too far left for a more moderate state. Rogers is another Republican who has been more willing to break with Trump. He has spoken out against Trump’s trade war with Canada and has called for an end to the Iran war. El-Sayed led by 4 points in a survey from Mitchell Research & Communications, 45.6 percent to 41.4 percent. It polled 682 likely voters October 1 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points. A Fox News poll showed an even closer race, giving El-Sayed just a 1-point lead, 50 percent to 49 percent. It was conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research from September 24-28 among 1,028 likely voters. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. Ohio Ohio, like Iowa, is a former midwestern battleground that has become more conservative in recent years but appears to be more competitive in this year’s elections. Trump won Ohio by about 11 points in 2024 but is now 21 points underwater, with 36 percent approving and 57 percent disapproving of him, per Civiqs. Senator Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill the seat vacated by Vice President JD Vance, is facing a challenge from Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown, who represented the state for nearly two decades before losing reelection in 2024. Brown held a 4-point lead in a Marist University poll, 48 percent to 44 percent, among 1,176 likely voters October 15-18, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points. An ActiVote poll, which surveyed 400 likely voters September 26-October 18, showed the two candidates tied at 50 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.9 percentage points. Husted has campaigned with Trump, though he has broken with the president in some instances, including voting against the anti-weaponization fund and calling for a quick end to the Iran war. Texas Texas’ reputation as a conservative stronghold is at risk as GOP Attorney General Ken Paxton faces a competitive challenge from Democratic state Representative James Talarico. Trump won Texas by nearly 14 points in 2024, but his approval has fallen to -21 points, with 36 percent approving and 57 percent disapproving, according to Civiqs. Paxton is a close Trump ally, and the president boosted his primary challenge against longtime Republican Senator John Cornyn by giving him an endorsement. Trump has rallied behind Paxton, and the MAGA Inc. PAC, which is aligned with the president, has invested heavily in the race as polls show Talarico with a slight edge. A YouGov poll showed Talarico up 2 points, 51 percent to 49 percent, among 1,458 likely voters October 8-16. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.4 percentage points. A poll from the University of Houston also gave Talarico a 2-point lead, 48 percent to 46 percent, among 2,000 likely voters October 10-14, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.19 percentage points. Democrats’ Chances of Flipping the Senate, Two Weeks Before Election Day Democrats have emerged as favorites in prediction markets. On Kalshi, Democrats had a 63 percent chance of winning a majority on Tuesday, while they had a 65 percent chance on Polymarket. Prediction markets let traders buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real-money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always predict the future accurately. What Happens Next Trump’s approval rating will remain closely watched as an important gauge of the electorate’s mood in the final stretch of campaign season. His approval could be shaped by issues like the economy and cost of living over the coming weeks, as candidates continue to make their final pitches to voters ahead of the midterms. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: Trump is unpopular in seven states with toss-up Senate races ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, according to polling data.
news.author: Andrew Stanton

news.title: Sunny Hostin re-visits 'problematic' Kamala Harris answer on 'The View' as hosts question her 2028 potential
news.text: "The View" co-host Sunny Hostin revisited her widely-discussed 2024 question to former Vice President Kamala Harris during an event on Monday, calling the former Democratic presidential nominee's answer and refusal to distance herself from former President Joe Biden at the time "problematic." Brian Teta, the talk show's executive producer and host of its "Behind the Table" podcast, selected the moment as Hostin's most memorable on the show. He said it was a "seminal moment" in the 2024 election cycle. Hostin described the question as a "gift" and said she thought Harris would have to distance herself from Biden because of his approval ratings at the time. She also said "The View" was the perfect venue to ask the question, calling the liberal show's audience "her people." "I actually thought the answer was going to be, you know, ‘We had a lot of wins in this administration. I was there for those wins, but I, as a woman of color, as a child of immigrants, as I have a different lived experience, and I intend to bring that lived experience with me into the White House. I will do this. I will do that. I will do this. I will do that. I will do that.’ That was what I was expecting. I was not expecting, 'Not a single thing comes to mind.' And I knew honestly when she said it that it was really problematic," Hostin said. KAMALA HARRIS CALLS TO EXPAND SUPREME COURT, ADD STATES IF DEMS TAKE CONGRESS The co-hosts noted that the moment was discussed in books published after the 2024 election, including Harris' memoir, "107 Days," and was also featured in a political ad for President Donald Trump. In "107 Days," Harris wrote that she had no idea she had just "pulled the pin on a hand grenade," with her answer to Hostin's question. She wrote that her staff was beside themselves. "Stationed at various places around the set, my staff were beside themselves. Political operatives have an eye to see a moment, and I could kick myself for giving the other side that moment. During the commercial break, while I was having a bit of fun with some young students I’d noticed in the audience who were obviously playing hooky, offering to write notes to their teachers after the show, Opal [Vadhan] passed me a note from our team, telling me to return to that question and mention that a big difference would be that I would put a Republican in my cabinet," she wrote in her book. 'THE VIEW' CO-HOSTS CAST DOUBT ON KAMALA HARRIS VIABILITY AS 2028 CANDIDATE Teta and the co-hosts said they all knew her response was going to be a problem. Co-host Ana Navarro said Harris' staff "ran" because staff members knew immediately that Harris needed to return to the question and address her answer. KAMALA HARRIS FACES DEMOCRATIC DOUBTS OVER 2028 AS ALLIES PUSH BACK ON CLAIMS SHE’S SQUANDERED HER CHANCE During the show on Friday, both Navarro and Haines said they wouldn't tell Harris not to run, but questioned if she would be the best option for the Democratic Party. "If the Democrats want to win, I don't think she's the right candidate because I think the Democrats have been screaming for new energy. They've been saying we need something new to combat this. This would be her third time on this ballot. From the first time when she didn't ... she was out really early when she ran, and then the time with Biden, this would be the third time. People are clamoring for fresh energy, and there's a lot of candidates," Haines said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Co-host Joy Behar has said on several occasions that she doesn't think the U.S. would elect a woman as president, citing Harris and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton's losses to Trump. She has said the 2028 Democratic presidential nominee should be a man if the party wants to win. Hostin questioned whether president would be the right position for Harris during an April episode of "The View" and said she wished Harris had pursued a run for California governor. "This goes right to the heart of what the Media Research Center has been arguing to the FCC about for months now. The View knowingly operates as a propaganda arm for the Democratic Party and for Democratic candidates," NewsBusters associate editor Nicholas Fondacaro told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Sunny openly admitted that her intention with the question was to help Kamala with what she felt was a layup question that would lead to a slam-dunk answer. This incident was an abuse of ABC's privileged access to the public broadcast spectrum."
news.summary: Sunny Hostin called Kamala Harris' answer on "The View" a "problematic" moment, revealing exactly what she expected the vice president to say.
news.author: Hanna Panreck

news.title: Trump rallies in Kansas as rising farm costs fuel Republican concerns about voter turnout
news.text:
TOPEKA, Kan. (AP) — Fifth-generation Kansas farmer Glenn Brunkow describes this time of year as “go time,” when farmers are combining fields, hauling crops to town and moving livestock from summer pastures to their winter homes.

But this harvest season, they’re doing it with diesel prices more than $2.50 per gallon higher than a year ago, adding to financial pressures from rising costs, unpredictable markets and shrinking profits.

“It seems like it’s coming at us from all directions,” said Brunkow, president of the Kansas Farm Bureau.

The economic strain is becoming a growing political concern for Republicans in states they have long dominated. President Donald Trump appeared in Kansas on Monday and will go to Iowa later in the week, the latest in a series of stops where he’s trying to energize his base in the final weeks before the midterm elections.

“In this election, I’m asking you to pretend please that I’m on the ballot,” Trump told the Kansas crowd. He spoke for over an hour and a half, with protesters interrupting him several times.

The visits come as Republicans pour money into Senate races in Kansas, Nebraska and Iowa amid concerns about voter enthusiasm. The anxiety may be especially notable in Kansas — a state Trump won by 16 percentage points against Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024 — as Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces a tough challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton. Democrats have not won a Senate election in Kansas in 94 years.

Hamilton, the founder of the nation’s largest United Methodist church, has attracted Republican support in his Senate bid, including endorsements from two former GOP governors. In a video statement ahead of Trump’s visit, Hamilton said it was “an honor” to welcome a sitting president to Kansas.

“I want Kansans to know that if you voted for the president, you also have a place in my campaign,” he added.

Brunkow, whose organization endorsed Marshall, said he’s been asked many times whether the economic frustrations could drive Republican farmers to vote for Democrats.

“I don’t think it necessarily does that,” Brunkow said. “But I think it dampens the enthusiasm for agriculture producers to get to the polls.”

Republican voters’ frustrations with the party have deepened

Don Hineman, a western Kansas rancher and former Republican state House majority leader, said he’s seeing growing frustration among GOP voters beyond just farmers, including some who have supported Trump in multiple elections.

He said farmers understand that Trump’s tariffs have hurt their businesses and are upset over the ongoing war with Iran. Immigration has also become a source of concern, particularly after recent immigration raids in western Kansas that resulted in the detention of more than 100 people.

“We need a secure border — we can all agree on that,” Hineman said. “But we also need workable immigration policy that provides the workforce that the United States has always depended on and will always continue to need.”

Hineman said the traditional Republican argument in Kansas — that electing Democrats would empower the party’s liberal wing — is losing its effectiveness with some voters, including himself.

“I am tired of being persuaded by charges that the boogeyman is going to get us,” he said. “I am so fed up with the Republican Party and their willingness to play sycophant to our current commander in chief that I’m willing to consider alternatives.”

Debbie Geneva, 61, of Nortonville, Kansas, said she was impressed by Hamilton after he visited a local market to meet people, something she hasn’t seen Marshall do. She’s never voted for a Democrat, she said, but remains undecided about the Senate race.

“I’ve never voted for a Democrat in my entire life, so that’s a little scary for me to be undecided,” said Geneva. “I told one of my friends that, and they can’t believe it, but that’s just the way I feel right now.”

Geneva said rising costs for healthcare and everyday expenses have added to her frustrations.

“And then of course the trade agreements,” she added. “The Republicans haven’t done the Midwest any favors with that.”

Farmers face a financial squeeze

Farmers have spent months feeling the squeeze as costs for inputs like diesel, fertilizer and seed have soared due to refinery constraints and supply disruptions tied to the Iran war.

Diesel averaged $6.30 per gallon nationwide on Friday, more than 70% higher than a year ago, according to motor club AAA. The surge has been especially painful during harvest season, when farmers depend heavily on fuel to operate machinery and transport crops.

“This is a time of year when we use a lot of fuel, and there just isn’t much we can do,” Brunkow said. “The margins are tight, and anything that cuts into that margin really hurts.”

The U.S. Department of Agriculture projects that net farm income will decline by 2.6% this year as production expenses rise by 4.5%. Fuel and oil expenses alone are expected to jump nearly 30%, according to the agency’s September forecast.

Trump said Monday night that the Department of Agriculture will be launching a new harvest fuel relief program, claiming it will provide $8 billion in support for farmers to offset diesel costs.

“When Republicans win, we will pass even more funding for our farmers. We love our farmers,” Trump said.

Earlier this month, Trump signed an executive order to ease limits on the tax-free use of red-dyed diesel, a decision he said would save “millions” for farmers. That came after a $12 billion aid package for farmers announced by the Trump administration in December.

But those efforts have not erased frustrations among some farmers who expected their financial outlook to improve under Trump.

Brunkow said many farmers “thought it would be better” under Trump.

“He’s made some unforced errors,” said Brunkow.

Concerns spread beyond Kansas

Trump will travel on Thursday to Iowa, where Republicans are defending competitive races for governor and Senate. The state, which Trump has carried in three consecutive presidential elections, is another agricultural stronghold where economic frustrations have become part of the political debate.

In Nebraska, Senate Republicans have poured nearly $15 million into a race between GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts and independent candidate Dan Osborn, an unprecedented amount for a state Trump won by 20 percentage points in 2024.

David McIntosh, president of the influential Club for Growth, said his group has kept a close eye on the heavy agriculture states since summer and acknowledged concerns about a drop-off in enthusiasm. His group is spending millions of dollars for GOP candidates in Kansas, Nebraska and elsewhere.

“Farmers are squeezed between higher input prices and less of an international market because of retaliatory tariffs,” McIntosh said. “The economic environment has not been good.”

Democrats, meanwhile, see an opportunity in the economic frustrations, even in states where they have struggled to win statewide elections.

Former Sen. Jon Tester, a Montana Democrat who lost reelection in 2024, said there is “no doubt” that Democrats will perform better than expected in agricultural states.

“These guys got to pay bills at the end of the month, and for a number of months now it’s been hard to do,” said Tester. “This is way beyond politics.”

news.title: Donald Trump's Christianity Remarks Draw Online Rebuke as Commenter Says He 'Spits in the Face of Christians!'
news.text: President Donald Trump has drawn criticism online after boasting about his support among Christian voters during a campaign rally in Park City, Kansas, on Monday, 19 October.One X commenter reportedly accused him of disrespecting believers, writing, 'This guy spits in the face of Christians!'Trump made the remarks while campaigning for Republican Senator Roger Marshall ahead of the 3 November US midterm elections.Marshall faces a competitive challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, a United Methodist pastor, as Republicans seek to retain control of the Senate.Trump's Christianity Remarks Spark Online CriticismSpeaking to supporters at Heartland Credit Union Arena, Trump highlighted his standing among religious voters, declaring, 'I have the all-time, in history, Christian vote.' He also said, 'I know more than anybody,' after referring to his support among evangelical and Christian voters.The president did not provide voting figures to substantiate his claim of historically high Christian support. The speech transcript also does not establish that he was claiming to know more about Christian teachings than anybody else.Trump then recounted remarks he attributed to an unnamed pastor from Dallas, Texas. According to the president, the pastor acknowledged that Trump might not read the Bible as frequently as others or know every passage, but praised his leadership and predicted that he would guide Christianity into a period of significant change.The prediction was presented as the pastor's assessment rather than Trump's own original declaration. Trump subsequently said the pastor had turned out to be right, although he did not identify the religious leader or provide independent confirmation of the conversation.The remarks drew criticism in social media reactions quoted by Dagens.com. One X user reportedly wrote, 'This guy spits in the face of Christians!,' accusing the president of showing disrespect towards the religious community whose support he frequently highlights.Other reported reactions were similarly critical. One commenter described Trump as 'delusional', while another declared, 'Just this comment alone should get him impeached.'The comments reflect criticism from individual social media users rather than an established consensus among Christian voters. Dagens.com did not identify the accounts behind the quoted reactions.The publication also cited criticism of Trump's wider political record, including his administration's spending priorities. However, those accusations were separate from the immediate controversy over his religious remarks and were not independently substantiated in the report.No response from Trump's representatives or a named Christian organisation was included in Dagens.com's account. The available reporting also does not establish how widely the criticism circulated or whether it influenced voters' perceptions of the president.Trump's Christianity Remarks Come Amid Competitive Kansas Senate RaceThe religious comments came during a campaign appearance intended to strengthen Republican support in Kansas, where Marshall is seeking another Senate term. His Democratic challenger, Hamilton, is a prominent United Methodist pastor who has campaigned on concerns about household costs, healthcare and political divisions.Hamilton's religious background adds context to Trump's references to Christian voters during the rally. However, there is no verified evidence linking the reported X criticism to Hamilton's campaign or suggesting that the comments represent the views of his supporters.Kansas has traditionally favoured Republicans in presidential elections. According to the Associated Press, Trump defeated Democrat Kamala Harris in the state by approximately 16 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election.Despite that margin, the Senate contest has become competitive. The RealClearPolling average covering surveys conducted between 8 September and 14 October placed Marshall at 46.0 per cent and Hamilton at 45.7 per cent, a difference of just 0.3 percentage points.The close polling has attracted attention because Democrats have not won a US Senate election in Kansas since 1932. George McGill was the last Democrat elected to the chamber from the state, winning re-election 94 years ago.Economic concerns have also influenced the campaign. Reuters reported that rising fuel and agricultural costs have become important issues for Kansas voters, particularly in rural communities facing financial pressure.Trump's appearance formed part of a wider campaign effort to mobilise Republican voters ahead of the midterms. He is also scheduled to visit Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday, 22 October, as the party campaigns in states with competitive elections.While the Kansas rally highlighted Trump's continued emphasis on Christian voter support, the reported online criticism focused on his language about religion and leadership.Whether those reactions will have any measurable political impact remains unclear, with no polling or other evidence establishing a connection between the comments and voter intentions.

news.title: Inflation has hit a new group of goods: Trump merch
news.text:
As American consumers continue to battle a cost of living crisis that has made everything from groceries to fuel more expensive, new analysis has found that the price of official Donald Trump merchandise is soaring too.

Trump returned to office pledging a new “golden age” but, with inflation still stubbornly high at 3.7 percent and the Iran war driving up gas prices, only a minority of voters appear to believe he has delivered. 

The latest pre-midterms poll from The Washington Post/ABC News/Ipsos put the president’s approval rating at just 33 percent and found that 37 percent of the public would rather see a Democrat in charge of the economy.

A survey by The Washington Sun, using the WayBack Machine to review archived webpages, has now found that the cost of a red MAGA cap, one of the icons of Trump’s political project, has risen from $25 during his first presidential campaign a decade ago to $55 now – a 120 percent rise. 

As recently as the 2024 election, when they were retailing for $40, Trump campaign officials were telling The Independent they had shipped more than 2 million hats as people cheerily declared their support for the Republican when he ran against Kamala Harris.

However, in August this year, former GOP congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene claimed the cap was inadvertently becoming a symbol of the president’s waning popularity, observing on X: “I can’t remember the last time I saw someone wearing a MAGA hat or Trump shirt.” 

The president has long shown a willingness to slap his name on everything from golden hi-top sneakers to watches, digital trading cards, guitars and even Bibles – with varying degrees of success – and the red MAGA cap is not the only item whose price tag has received a recent mark-up.

The Sun’s analysis found that Trump’s “Victory 47” perfume and cologne – which debuted in February 2024 at $99, before having their packaging redesigned and selling for $199 – is now going for $249 a bottle. 

The outlet notes that the product most directly impacted by the economy is the president’s range of gold and silver medallions, the price of which is reportedly tied to the value of those precious metals, meaning it can fluctuate dramatically.

The Independent has reached out to the Trump Organization for comment. 

Todd Belt, a professor of political management at George Washington University in Washington, D.C., pointed out that the president’s supporters have traditionally been prepared to pay more for his merchandise, which they wear as a tribal uniform, signifying their loyalty.

MAGA Republicans sees Trump-branded clothing as an important means of expressing their “allegiance to somebody who they think is tough, somebody who they think says the types of things that other people aren’t willing to say,” Belt said.

However, the professor also suggested it could be seen as “tone deaf” to be hawking merch at high prices just now given the public’s affordability concerns and the frequency of headlines about the president and his family allegedly using the presidency to enrich themselves while voters struggle to make ends meet.

The prospect of hard times coming for the Trump merchandise sector was foretold in August when a massive Trump superstore in Knoxville, Tennessee, was forced to close its doors because shoppers were staying away, even with a 50 percent discount on offer.

The owner of a similar venture, Trump Town USA in Boones Mill, Virginia, likewise admitted to the straitened circumstances in September, telling The Wall Street Journal: “Today, the economy is just not worth a c*** anymore.”
news.summary: Price hikes mean President Donald Trump’s signature red MAGA cap is now retailing for $55, up from $25 a decade ago, according to new analysis

news.title: Mary Peltola Is Pulling Ahead in the Final Stretch Against Dan Sullivan
news.text: Alaska Democratic candidate Mary Peltola has pulled ahead of Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in a string of recent polls of their critical Senate race, but the lead remains narrow. Alaska has become a prime pickup opportunity for Democrats as they hope to ride a blue wave back into majorities in both the House and Senate. Peltola, a former Congresswoman in the state, has proven to be a strong candidate and the GOP has faced headwinds as President Donald Trump's approval ratings continue to slide along with voters' views on the economy and the Iran war. Democrats need to defend all of their Senate seats and flip four others to take the majority in the upper chamber. Only one state—Maine—features a race where an incumbent Republican is trying to defend their seat in a state that Kamala Harris won in 2024. Democrats have had to broaden their battlefield to target states where Trump won by double digits in 2024, including Alaska. While the state last elected a Democrat to the Senate in 2008, it has not backed a Democrat for the White House since 1964 and has long been considered a safe zone for Republicans. Newsweek reached out to Peltola’s campaign and Sullivan’s campaign by email for comment on Tuesday morning. Peltola Holds a Narrow Lead Peltola held a 44 percent to 42 percent lead over Sullivan, who is endorsed by Trump, in a Rasmussen Reports poll conducted between October 12 and October 15. The survey polled 775 Alaska likely voters and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points, carrying a 95 percent level of confidence. An InsiderAdvantage poll conducted between October 9 and October 10 gave the former congresswoman an even wider margin of 5 percent over Sullivan, with the Democrat obtaining the support of 48 percent of the 1,200 likely voters surveyed and the Republican 43 percent in a four-way ballot. Two other Republican candidates, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. and Gerald L. Heikes, received 1.7 percent and 2.2 percent of the vote, respectively, while 5.3 percent of likely voters were undecided. The poll’s margin of error was plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. In a hypothetical second round of voting in that poll, where Sullivan Jr. and Heikes were eliminated, 50.1 percent of voters threw their support behind Peltola, while 48.0 percent backed the incumbent Republican. Peltola’s Lead Has Been Consistent Over Past Few Weeks Other polling conducted this month has also pointed in Peltola’s direction, but the contest appears to remain extraordinarily tight. Public Policy Polling’s survey from October 14 to October 15 put Peltola at 48 percent and Sullivan at 47 percent, while Alaska Survey Research found Peltola leading 47 percent to 45 percent in an October 1 to October 3 four-way survey. The first poll was conducted among 578 registered voters, while the second surveyed 1,512 likely voters and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. A Quantus Insights poll conducted from September 28 to September 30 showed the two candidates tied at 47 percent, with the gap between the two far smaller than the survey’s margin of error. Peltola and Sullivan Clash Over Iran War, Energy Production and Fuel Prices Over the past few months, Peltola and Sullivan have traded increasingly pointed attacks, with both campaigns seeking to cast the other candidate as out of step with Alaskans. Those divisions were on full display during an October 15 debate, as the candidates clashed over the war with Iran, energy production and the high costs of fuel in the state. Peltola sought to draw a direct line between the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the financial pressures facing Alaskans, accusing Sullivan of voting 14 times in favor of the war. Trump, who has said the war is necessary to prevent Iran from having a nuclear weapon, has endorsed Sullivan and traveled to the state last week to support Sullivan’s campaign. The Republican incumbent, meanwhile, argued that greater energy production in Alaska could help bring prices down and attacked Peltola’s record in Congress, saying the former representative had voted against producing more Alaskan energy. Foreign policy was another point of contention. Both candidates opposed the prospect of importing Russian diesel, with Sullivan saying the plan was “not a good idea” and Peltola describing buying fuel from a “known adversary”—Russia’s leader Vladimir Putin—as a “terrible” and “foolish” decision. Peltola also used the debate to argue for continued support for Ukraine and criticized the Trump administration’s treatment of the U.S. traditional allies. How Alaska's Senate Race Matters in the Midterms Democrats have seized on Alaska as a prime flip opportunity in 2026. They need to flip four GOP-held seats to gain the majority and will need to flip at least two seats in states that Trump won by double digits in 2024. Alaska has become a prime target falling along these lines, along with Texas, Ohio and Iowa. Peltola has won a statewide election before and is running as a centrist, targeting independent voters and disillusioned moderate Republicans who might not back a candidate who has been endorsed by Trump. Political forecaster the Cook Political Report rates the Senate race as a toss-up and Sabato's Crystal Ball has shifted the state to the Leans Democrat category. Vote Counting Might Take Weeks, Delaying Race’s Results Even after voters cast their ballots on November 3, a winner in the Alaska Senate race may take weeks to be declared. The state uses ranked choice voting for federal and state general elections, with first-choice results reported initially and additional ranked-choice tabulation conducted if necessary. Close elections can take up to 15 days to resolve because Alaska continues receiving eligible absentee ballots during its postelection counting window. With Peltola and Sullivan separated by such narrow margins in the latest polling, the state could be one of the Senate map’s key unresolved races well beyond election night. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Matthew Robinson and Geoffrey Rowland.
news.summary: With two weeks to go before Election Day, Mary Peltola has gained a narrow but solid lead over Dan Sullivan, latest polling shows.
news.author: Giulia Carbonaro

news.title: First Day Of Early Voting In Texas Breaks Records In Blue, Urban Counties
news.text:
Two Democratic areas in Texas posted record-breaking first-day early voting numbers Monday, which could spell trouble for Republicans. 

Dallas and Harris County had more voters than ever when early voting began Monday, which was a good sign for Democratic Texas Senate nominee James Talarico. Judge Clay Jenkins, who has access to official data from the Dallas County Elections Department, reported that 76,069 voters showed up in Dallas County, which surpassed the previous record of 60,573 voters in 2020. 

The number of registered voters in Dallas surged from 1,398,469 in 2020 to 1,463,708 this year, a 4.7% rise. 

Former Vice President Kamala Harris won Dallas County by a 60.1% to 38.1% margin in the 2024 presidential election, according to Politico. Former Democratic Texas Senate nominee Colin Allred won the county by 29 points against Republican Texas Sen. Ted Cruz. (RELATED: Republicans Pour $30,000,000 Into Ken Paxton’s Campaign During Final Stretch Of Red-State Race)

@DallasElections For context the first day vote is up significantly in Dallas County when you compare it to the last Trump midterm in 2018. 2018- 59,388 2026-76,079— Clay Lewis Jenkins (@JudgeClayJ) October 20, 2026

The number of voters in Dallas County already surpassed turnout during the 2024 presidential election, according to The Political HQ. 

 The Harris County Elections Department recorded over 100,000 in-person voters. As of 3:30 pm central time, over 70,000 voters had been processed, which surpassed the previous record of 63,188 votes recorded in the 2018 midterm elections. Harris County includes the city of Houston. 

“Harris County has broken the record for first-day early voting turnout in a midterm election!As of 3:30 p.m., 70K+ voters have been processed, surpassing the previous record of 63,188 set in 2018, with 3.5 hours remaining,” the Harris County Elections Department said on X. 

Day 1 of Early Voting: As of October 19, 2026, #HarrisCounty has recorded 104.6K + total In-Person Early Voters for the November 3 General & Special Elections. 🗳️✅ #harrisvotes https://t.co/vXRFWBtTSs— Harris County Elections Department (@HarrisVotes) October 20, 2026

The county’s number of registered voters rose 14.7%, from 2,357,199 in 2018 to 2,702,952 this year, according to county data. 

Harris won Harris County by a five-point margin, 51.9% to 46.5%, according to Politico. 

Over 22,000 voters turned out in El Paso County, the second-highest turnout number on record for the first day of early voting. The historically blue county had its highest ever first-day voter turnout in the 2018 midterm election when 24,449 were recorded. Harris won in El Paso County by 15 points, according to Politico. 

Collin County, Denton County and Tarrant County reported increased voter turnout in comparison to the previous election in 2022, which are all historically Republican counties. Collins County reported over 34,000 voters on the first day of early voting, which was well above the roughly 19,000 voters on the first day of early voting in 2022, according to Fox 4 KDFW, a local Fox affiliate. 

The county reported approximately 43,000 voters on the first day of early voting in 2024, according to Fox 4 KDFW. 

Denton County reported over 34,000 voters on the first day, which surpassed turnout in 2018 and 2022. 

Republican PACs spent over $326 million to support Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton while he fell behind Talarico in the polls. Talarico led by an average of 2.2 points as of Tuesday, according to RealClearPolling. 

Paxton told donors in leaked audio that the Iran war and gas prices caused his campaign to struggle. 

The PACs spent unprecedented amounts in other red states, including Kansas, South Dakota, South Carolina and Iowa.

news.title: Elissa Slotkin’s ‘Deterrence Message’ Has a Name, and It Isn’t ‘Defending Democracy’
news.text:
Welcome to Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. Today is the National Day on Writing, which for some of us is just called Tuesday.

My calendar says it’s Chicken and Waffles Day, Day on Writing, Youth Confidence Day, Brandied Fruit Day, International Chefs Day, International Sloth Day, and World Osteoporosis Day. So write something bold, cook something fried, follow it with brandied fruit, and then go full sloth on the couch. Your bones can file a complaint tomorrow.

Today in History:

1803: The Senate ratified the Louisiana Purchase, doubling the size of the country for about 3 cents an acre.1818: The United States and Britain signed the Convention of 1818, setting the 49th parallel as much of the border with Canada.1910: Harland and Wolff launched the hull of Olympic, the older sister of Titanic, in Belfast.1944: Gen. Douglas MacArthur waded ashore at Leyte, making good on his promise to return to the Philippines.1947: A House committee opened hearings into alleged communist influence in Hollywood, a probe that gave birth to the Hollywood blacklist.1952: Kenya’s British colonial governor declared a state of emergency over the Mau Mau uprising.1967: Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin shot their famous Bigfoot footage at Bluff Creek, Calif.1968: Jacqueline Kennedy married Greek shipping tycoon Aristotle Onassis on the island of Skorpios.1973: President Richard Nixon ordered the firing of special prosecutor Archibald Cox, and Attorney General Elliot Richardson and Deputy Attorney General William Ruckelshaus resigned rather than carry it out. History remembers it as the “Saturday Night Massacre.”1973: Queen Elizabeth II opened the Sydney Opera House.1977: A plane crash near Gillsburg, Miss., killed Lynyrd Skynyrd’s Ronnie Van Zant, Steve Gaines, and Cassie Gaines.1981: Members of the Black Liberation Army and the Weather Underground robbed a Brink’s truck in Nanuet, N.Y., killing a guard and two police officers.1991: The Oakland Hills firestorm tore through the hills above Oakland, Calif., killing 25 people and destroying thousands of homes.2004: The Boston Red Sox beat the New York Yankees in Game 7 to complete the first comeback from a 3-0 deficit in baseball postseason history.2011: Libyan rebels captured and killed Moammar Gadhafi near his hometown of Sirte.

Birthdays Today include: Christopher Wren, architect (St. Paul’s Cathedral); John Dewey, philosopher and education reformer; Bela Lugosi, actor (Dracula); Jelly Roll Morton, jazz pianist and composer (“Jelly Roll Blues”); Art Buchwald, humor columnist; Joyce Brothers, psychologist and TV personality; Mickey Mantle, Hall of Fame center fielder (New York Yankees); Jerry Orbach, actor (Law & Order, Dirty Dancing); Wanda Jackson, rockabilly singer (“Let’s Have a Party”); Tom Petty, rock singer-songwriter (“Free Fallin’,” “Refugee”); Keith Hernandez, first baseman and broadcaster (New York Mets, Seinfeld); Danny Boyle, director (Trainspotting, Slumdog Millionaire); Viggo Mortensen, actor (The Lord of the Rings); Kamala Harris, former vice president; Snoop Dogg, rapper (Doggystyle); John Krasinski, actor and director (The Office, A Quiet Place). 

If today’s your birthday, too, many happy returns. Go easy on the brandied fruit.

Democrats have spent the better part of a decade wailing about “weaponized government.” It turns out they never objected to the weapon; they objected to who held it. Some evidence of this is in an interesting piece from Glenn Reynolds in the New York Post this morning:

Now Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), speaking at the University of Chicago, is calling for targeted prosecutions of Trump staffers. Slotkin observed that while Trump has presidential immunity, the people around him do not. She wants those prosecutions to scare away young conservatives who might want to go into politics. “I want them to be like, ‘Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems I don’t want, and so let me avoid participating in that.’ I want that deterrence message sent.”In the old days, politicians used to encourage young people to go into politics on either side in the name of civic engagement.The response was swift — and negative: “Sen. Slotkin, a self-avowed ‘defender of democracy,’ told me and other conservative students that we should live in fear of political persecution if we dare serve our country in the Trump administration,” wrote University of Chicago student Michael Bicksel on X. “Sadly for her, we will never be intimidated by her Bolshevik-style tactics.”

Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) calls it “deterrence”? Let’s try to find a more accurate label, and let’s start with the track record.

Glenn mentions Barack Obama’s IRS sitting on Tea Party groups’ applications for tax-exempt status. Here’s a fresher one: Last week, Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) released documents showing that Jack Smith’s team and the Biden Justice Department scooped up data on at least 639,000 Republican donors, voters, and supporters. That haul included people who bought red MAGA hats — their names, their purchases, and the addresses where the hats were shipped.

That's right: The federal government, in the middle of a criminal investigation, wanted to know where you live because you bought a hat. If you’d donated a few bucks, it wanted your credit card information, too.

So when Slotkin talks about prosecutions that send a message, nobody on the right needs her to draw a picture. We’ve seen the picture already.

Recommended: The Democrats’ Lead in the Polls Is Not As Solid As You Think 

Slotkin isn’t alone in wanting to make examples of conservatives. Jonathan Turley drew a parallel to Michael Sherwin, the federal prosecutor who led the early January 6 cases, who told CBS News the Justice Department wanted to send a message with its harsh treatment of Trump supporters.

Now, Slotkin insists she meant only accountability for officials who break the law, and she wants lawyers who abuse the justice system to answer for it through their bar status. Fine. But look at who she wants to deter. If she wanted to deter lawbreaking, she’d aim the message at lawbreakers. Instead, she aimed it at kids coming out of school who might want a job in the Trump administration. The goal she stated was fewer young conservatives in government, not less crime. That’s the tell, and no amount of cleanup on X erases it.

The irony is thick enough to spread on toast. When the Justice Department looked into Slotkin over her video telling troops to refuse “illegal orders,” she called it intimidation. As RedState’s Teri Christoph pointed out, Slotkin said at the time, “Facts matter little, but the threat matters quite a bit.” She understood exactly how the threat of prosecution worked when she was the target. She just doesn’t mind it when the target wears a red hat.

One might call this a "chilling effect," if one wanted to be gentle about it. I prefer not to. I’ve pointed out in previous columns that for all their charges of us being “Nazis,” it’s the Left that is actually using Nazi tactics, and what Slotkin is calling for is of a piece with that. (Hey, Elissa — 1933 Berlin called, and it wants its tactics back.)

The Nazis didn’t need to arrest every opponent. They needed to make examples. They needed to make opposition expensive enough that ordinary people chose to sit it out. In 1933, among its first moves, the new regime purged the civil service of the “politically unreliable.” The officials it fired mattered less than the lesson everyone else learned: Keep your head down and stay out of it.

Now reread Slotkin’s own words: “Let me avoid participating in that.” She didn’t stumble into describing that outcome; she described it as her goal. Michael Bicksel went with “Bolshevik,” and he’s not wrong, either. The Bolsheviks and the Nazis disagreed on plenty, but both understood that you don’t have to jail a whole generation if you can scare it into staying home. Now, I could pull the old saying about “Accuse the other side of that which you are guilty” to back this up. Interesting that there are so many arguments about the origins of that line, some attributing it to Joseph Goebbels and some to Lenin, Marx, and Saul Alinsky. It seems applicable to all of them.

This is the correct label: political intimidation. Persecution, if Slotkin ever gets the power to follow through. “Deterrence” is just the word she uses when she’d rather not say it out loud. And it’s the same Nazism the left, Slotkin included, so loudly decries.

The good news is that this kind of deterrence only works on people who let it. 

Reynolds has pointed out for years that tactics like these don’t build trust in the justice system. Rather, they burn it down, and he’s right to warn that this road leads somewhere far uglier. That’s because this was never about justice. It’s about power, and about making sure the next generation of conservatives never gets near it. Slotkin just had the poor judgment to say so on camera.

Slotkin, in the end, isn't "defending democracy." She's fighting for Democrats. No shock to me she doesn't know, or at least acknowledge, the difference.

news.title: Donald Trump Asked Texas For Five More Republicans. Voters Might Have Other Plans.
news.text:
Johnny Garcia, the Democratic nominee in Texas’ 35th congressional district, spent one of the last mornings before the start of early voting meeting with veterans over breakfast tacos and boxed coffee at a VFW hall in San Antonio’s Southside. That’s not surprising for a candidate running in a place known as “Military City, USA.” What is surprising? In a district Donald Trump would have carried by 11 points in 2024, a C-SPAN camera was there too, to capture the scene in what is shaping up to be one of the more unexpectedly competitive House races of 2026.

It wasn’t supposed to be this close. The 35th is one of five districts that were redrawn last summer to replace incumbent Democrats with Republicans, as part of President Donald Trump’s effort to preserve his party’s House majority through a wave of mid-decade redistricting. Kamala Harris carried Rep. Greg Casar’s old 35th—which extended from Austin to San Antonio—by 34 points. The almost entirely new 35th, stretching south and east of the city into rural counties of South Texas, is solidly Republican territory. Casar moved to the neighboring 37th district, which includes his Austin base, but the race for his old seat is tight. Fox News and the Cook Political Report have shifted the race from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican.” Trump recently visited San Antonio, in part to shore up support for Garcia’s Republican opponent, Carlos de la Cruz. And the Democratic group House Majority PAC recently announced $1.2 million in spending on a race its polling showed was within the margin of error.

What changed?

“The district woke up, on both sides of the aisle—I’m meeting more fed-up Republicans than I ever have here,” Garcia told me when we spoke after the event. A soft-spoken, self-described “old school Democrat” from San Antonio, Garcia has a background that’s helped insulate him against standard Republican attacks: He spent nearly two decades as a Bexar County sheriff’s deputy before entering the race, and has worked as a SWAT team hostage negotiator.

Leaning forward in a folding chair, wearing a white Stetson he removed only to thank an older woman for showing up, Garcia rattled off a list of Trump administration policies and economic factors that have hammered people in his district—tariffs, the never-ending war with Iran, and the rising price of everything from groceries to child care to utility bills. The average age of first-time homeowners was now 40, he noted (he’s still a renter at age 39), and even modest comforts came with a higher cost.

“People just want to make it to Sunday to buy barbacoa and Big Red, and unfortunately, under this economy, it’s a whole lot harder to do so.”

Working-class, heavily Latino areas of San Antonio—and across South Texas—shifted hard toward Republicans over the last few election cycles. But Garcia told me Republicans in Washington had failed their electorate.

“We’re seeing a 16-point shift of Latinos coming back to the party—the folks that they thought were just going to vote for them up and down the ballot again this election cycle. The way Democrats and Biden failed us here on the border, Republicans are seeing them failing on the economic issues. The things that they promised are ultimately being kicked down the road.”

The 35th district isn’t the only place where Republicans’ redistricting ambitions are facing major headwinds. While Republicans are still likely to net seats in the state, it has become an increasingly expensive endeavor thanks largely to the president’s plummeting popularity among Latino voters.

The redistricting plan approved by state Republicans last summer was designed to pick up as many as five seats by eliminating Casar’s Austin seat, Rep. Al Green’s Houston seat, and Rep. Julie Johnson’s Dallas seat, and by making two Democratic seats in South Texas (held by Reps. Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez) more Republican. In response, Green and Johnson both tried to run in different districts and lost their primaries. Casar avoided a primary in a newly consolidated Austin district when Rep. Lloyd Doggett stepped aside. 

But Cuellar and Gonzalez, representing seats Trump carried by double digits, vowed to hold on, and they still might. The Congressional Leadership Fund, the campaign arm of the House GOP, recently cancelled $3 million worth of advertisements in Cuellar’s district, where the incumbent has weathered a bribery indictment (he was pardoned by Trump before the case could proceed and has denied wrongdoing) and consistently led his challenger. Gonzalez narrowly led Republican Eric Flores in the only public poll of his race. And while Republicans are still likely to pick up a seat in the Dallas area, Fox News shifted its rating of the newly gerrymandered 9th district near Houston from “solid Republican” to “likely Republican” last week, suggesting a tightening race between Republican Alex Mealer and Democrat Leticia Gutierrez.

Meanwhile, Democrats have a real shot at flipping a South Texas seat Republicans already hold—in the 15th district, where Rep. Monica de la Cruz (Carlos’ sister) is in a tight race with Democrat Bobby Pulido, a Tejano music star. Cook now considers that race a toss-up.

The Republican redistricting ploy is still unlikely, however, to prove to be a “dummymander”—a map that ends up costing the party seats by leaving Republicans more vulnerable in a wave. In part that’s because Republicans learned from their experience in 2012, when they did draw a dummymander that came back to bite them in 2018. That year, they lost 12 state House of representative seats and two congressional seats. The damage was compounded by the fact that it was suburban communities in the state’s largest metros—areas that had once helped sustain Republican rule—that shifted hardest toward Democrats in Trump’s first term. You could think of a dummymander as akin to building at sea level without accounting for climate change. “I told them that ICE does have a job to do, they have to make sure that we’re not allowing the flow of illegal drugs and human smuggling coming into our communities, [that] we’re actually going after the bad actors that should not be here in our communities,” he said. But, “it also doesn’t make any sense when they’re going after five-year-old Liam Ramoses and they’re targeting our construction sites, and they’re diminishing and depleting the workforce that’s ultimately working to make housing more affordable these days.”

The veterans and their advocates at the roundtable shared a litany of concerns about the administration, from the effects of DOGE at the Department of Veterans Affairs to the president’s efforts to intimidate critics like Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.). Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was a frequent target. He recently closed two Army command posts in a city where there are still hard feelings over the 2001 closure of Kelly Air Force Base.

“It’s clear as day that Pete Hegseth came into San Antonio and wanted to rip apart our armed forces here as a political stunt,” Garcia told them. The House majority, he told them, was more focused on protecting the secretary from impeachment than on passing legislation that would make people’s lives easier. When I asked Garcia whether he’d support impeachment, he demurred.

“My priority is making sure that that we’re tearing down these tariffs that are hurting 97 percent of small businesses and working class families,” he said. “My priority is making sure that we’re making permanent the ACA tax credits and subsidies that make health care affordable, and once we accomplish those two priorities on the agenda list, then we can look at everything else down the road.”

Garcia describes himself as a “troubleshooter,” not a “troublemaker.” His answer might not satisfy some members of his coalition demanding immediate accountability. But given how things were supposed to go in the district, it’s the kind of argument Democrats would love the chance to have.

news.title: El-Sayed Is the Kamala Harris of 2026
news.text:
For years, Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) has been remarkably upfront about just how far he wants government-run medicine to reach. Until recently. He’s trying to backtrack on it now, but we have the receipts. In podcast remarks from 2021 and 2022, he called for a taxpayer-funded universal health system that would cover gender-transition surgery for illegal immigrants.

According to a report from the Washington Free Beacon, El-Sayed made the remarks while working as a commentator and podcaster after his failed bid for Michigan governor. He pitched a "truly inclusive" universal healthcare entitlement that would include "care for transgender people" and "care for immigrants." The system, he said, should cover the "full gamut of health care that any and everyone would need." Run that through a plain-English filter, and you get coverage for illegal immigrants to get transgender procedures on the taxpayers' dime.

"A lot of the most difficult conversations break on the question of who deserves what care, right?" El-Sayed said in a Feb. 15, 2022, episode.

Recommended: The Democrats’ Lead in the Polls Is Not As Solid As You Think

Later in that same episode, he tried to get ahead of his critics. "The prime example that conservatives will impose on a conversation about Medicare for All will be 'Well, what do we do with the undocumented person who comes to this country and wants to get gender reassignment surgery on Medicare for All,'" he said.

According to El-Sayed, conservatives would push that example "because it captures a group of multiple marginalized people whom they want to cast as being undeserving." He then accused conservatives who object to footing the bill for these treatments of "the original sin of racism." So he correctly predicted the attack ad years in advance, and his game plan for answering it was to call anyone who runs it a racist.

Pardon me while I laugh.

It's worth revisiting exactly what Kamala said that got her into so much trouble.

"It is important that transgender individuals who rely on the state for care receive the treatment they need, which includes access to treatment associated with gender transition," Kamala wrote in a 2019 ACLU questionnaire. "That's why, as Attorney General, I pushed the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation to provide gender transition surgery to state inmates."

She also bragged that she "made sure they changed the policy in the state of California, so every transgender inmate in the prison system would have access to the medical care that they desired and needed." In her words, "it's a civil rights issue, it's a justice issue, and it's an issue of humanity."

Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers would be smart to take a page out of Trump’s playbook and run ads featuring these remarks during the campaign's final weeks.

news.title: ‘The Simpsons’ resurrects Apu after nearly a decade of silence
news.text:
Across 38 seasons of “The Simpsons,” the Halloween-themed “Treehouse of Horror” episodes have always been a treat of spooky stand-alone storylines. On Sunday, the show surprised viewers with a major resurrection: Apu, the beloved Kwik-E-Mart operator who had not been heard for the better part of a decade, spoke once again in Springfield.

He and his wife, Manjula, were back with a meaty plotline — and the voices of actual Indian American actors: Sunil Malhotra, a veteran voice-over artist, and Janina Gavankar (“The Morning Show”).

“Bringing Apu back feels like a reclamation. It truly IS his homecoming,” Malhotra and Gavankar said Sunday in a joint Instagram post.

Apu’s unheralded return is a remarkable twist to a yearslong discourse about how the character has represented a painful stereotype for some South Asian Americans. After a 2017 documentary by comedian Hari Kondabolu, “The Problem With Apu,” the character was largely exiled from the screen.

How a documentary on Apu became a turning point

In “The Problem With Apu,” Kondabolu, a self-described fan of the Fox show, tried to process his misgivings. He interviewed a slew of celebrities of South Asian origin, including Kal Penn, Utkarsh Ambudkar and Hasan Minhaj, about growing up with the character. They shared memories of being bullied and called “Apu” as an insult. Adding to their view of Apu as just a caricature was that Hank Azaria, a white actor, voiced him.

With the full name of Apu Nahasapeemapetilon Jr., he felt like the “forever foreigner, someone who represents Indians in the United States through this sole typology of being a convenience store owner, being a recent immigrant, having this heavy accent, being really limited in this sort of like American identity,” says Bhoomi Thakore, an assistant professor of sociology at the University of Connecticut. Thakore notes that Kondabolu’s film raised the notion that Apu was the only portrayal of an Indian character most people knew when he debuted in 1990.

Azaria stepped away from the role after the documentary, continuing to voice other “Simpsons” characters, as Apu fell silent, seen only in the background. Kondabolu, however, had never called for Apu to be canceled. On Monday, he praised “The Simpsons” for devising “a clever solution to all this” and hiring Malhotra and Gavankar.

“I’m also still proud of the public conversation about race and representation my documentary started,” he told The Associated Press in an emailed statement. “Finally, I’m hoping this stops all the hatemail in many languages that has been sent my way over the past decade.”

After years in the background, Apu appears here to stay

In a 2018 episode, “The Simpsons” responded to Kondabolu’s documentary by having Lisa Simpson bemoan how “something that started decades ago and was applauded and inoffensive is now politically incorrect. … What can you do?” The camera then panned to a framed photo of Apu. The gag was branded by some as weak for not directly addressing the controversy.

In a 2020 New York Times interview, Azaria, who by then hadn’t voiced Apu in a few years, announced he would bow out because “it just didn’t feel right.” Later that year, in response to racial reckoning demonstrations, “The Simpsons” announced it would no longer cast white voice actors as characters of color. The show then recast two Black characters, Carl Carlson and Dr. Julius Hibbert, with Black actors.

Kondabolu had not spoken with “The Simpsons” producers about Apu’s comeback, he confirmed to the AP, “but they didn’t owe me that.” And it does sound like Apu is here to stay.

“We love this character and wanted to bring him back in a smart, Simpsons-y way that allowed him to evolve,” executive producer Matt Selman said in a statement. “We’re excited by what Sunil has already brought to the role and look forward to seeing more of Apu in the future.”

Apu was also embraced by South Asians, despite the controversy

A few weeks after “The Simpsons” responded to the documentary, author and producer Amar Shah wrote a series of social media posts and then a Washington Post op-ed on why he felt mostly sentimental toward Apu. When he watched Apu, he thought of his own Indian father hard at work as a convenience store owner and how that shaped his Florida childhood.

“Apu even now is a character that I wouldn’t mind my kids seeing represented because they’ll see aspects of themselves and of their own grandparents,” says Shah, reflecting on his 2018 piece. “I can totally empathize with someone of South Asian origin having a different POV (point of view) than me but this is my childhood. This is my story.”

After watching this latest episode, Shah didn’t sense any significant difference with Malhotra’s performance.

“Obviously, there’s a different voice, tenor, texture and all that. But, the character is always going to be there, his genuine humanity,” Shah says. “I think if they had incorporated this change earlier, it would have been a lot better.”

At a time of anti-South Asian hate, Apu’s return is welcomed

Apu is being revived amid a climate of rising anti-South Asian and Indian hate. Stop AAPI Hate and other research groups have found online use of racist slurs and threats against South Asians and Indians have jumped in the past few years.

Texas Railroad Commission candidate Bo French, a Republican, recently posted a photo of South Asian University of Texas students cheering at a football game and called them “a problem.” Just last week, a man was charged with planning a mass shooting at a Hindu temple outside Chicago. Against that backdrop, Shah welcomes the show’s careful approach reincarnating the character.

“It’s great to see that the show has evolved in time and now, especially with the discrimination and, really, the targeting of South Asians and Indian Americans as of late — questioning our patriotism, our American identity and even whether we’re college football fans,” he says.

The return also coincides with much more representation of prominent South Asian Americans, such as actor and showrunner Mindy Kaling, and people who have broken barriers in office, like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

When Apu first appeared, says University of Virginia associate professor of media studies Shilpa Davé, he was one of the only consistent representations of South Asians on TV.

Now, she says, “South Asians have become a part of the landscape from ‘Bridgerton’ to … ‘Never Have I Ever’ and there’s a plethora of different kinds of representation.”

Associated Press journalist Mallika Sen contributed to this report.

news.title: 3 more Democrats slated to join summit on political future
news.text: Nine days after next month's midterm elections, three prominent Democrats who are widely believed to have presidential ambitions will join other potential 2028 party contenders in Denver to discuss the future of the party.Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, as well as Rep. Ro Khanna of California, are among the latest additions who plan to join the "What's Next" summit, according to an updated list of attendees first shared with CBS News. All three lawmakers identify as progressives, and all three have drawn national attention over their political ambitions in recent years. Booker ran for president in 2020 but dropped out before the first primary contests. Khanna has described himself as a "long-shot presidential candidate," and Van Hollen has acknowledged that he is "kicking the tires" on a possible 2028 run. The three have also introduced tax plans that could be precursors to 2028 platforms.The meeting will take place from Nov. 12 to 14, and is being hosted by Majority Democrats, a group formed last year by largely moderate elected officials and other high-profile Democrats who say they are "committed to reshaping and growing the Democratic Party." Chaired by Rep. Jake Auchincloss of Massachusetts, the organization says it aims to take lessons from the 2026 races into the upcoming presidential election, in part by bringing together leading voices from across different factions within the party."Democrats have talked a big game about building a 'big tent' that can hold onto a majority. The sad reality is, we were all hat, no cattle when it came time to live up to those ideals," said Matt Corridoni, a spokesperson for Majority Democrats. "What's Next is an opportunity for Democrats from every wing of the party to have the open and often difficult conversations we need to win in 2028."The three latest entrants join an initial lineup of other possible presidential candidates including former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Sens. Raphael Warnock of Georgia, Ruben Gallego of Arizona and Chris Murphy of Connecticut.Govs. Abigail Spanberger of Virginia and Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey plan to attend, as well as other members of Congress and political strategists.Democrats hope to win control of the House in November's midterm elections and carry the momentum into the 2028 presidential race. Many feel the party has not settled on a political identity after losing the White House in 2024, and moderate and progressive Democrats disagree on the party's direction.That split has not helped the party win over voters: In a February CBS News poll, most voters described the Democratic Party as "weak." Presidential contenders could begin launching their campaigns in the coming months, and some possible 2028 candidates have sought to raise their profile on the midterm trail, appearing alongside Democrats in key states. New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio Cortez and former Vice President Kamala Harris have both visited Michigan this fall to campaign with Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. California Gov. Gavin Newsom campaigned in New Hampshire last weekend with Rep. Chris Pappas, who is in a tight race for Senate. Organizers chose to hold the inaugural What's Next summit in Denver as it is one of the cities under consideration to host the 2028 Democratic National Convention. Over 2,000 people are expected to attend, according to a person familiar with the planning."Winning in 2028 will require us coming together to take the best ideas from every corner of the Democratic Party and forging them into an agenda that can build a durable majority and deliver for the American people," said executive director of Majority Democrats Rohan Patel.
news.summary: Sens. Cory Booker and Chris Van Hollen and Rep. Ro Khanna are among the latest additions to a post-midterm gathering in Denver, where Democrats will strategize about the future of the party.
