news.title: Trump rallies in Kansas as rising farm costs fuel Republican concerns about voter turnout
news.text:
TOPEKA, Kan. (AP) — Fifth-generation Kansas farmer Glenn Brunkow describes this time of year as “go time,” when farmers are combining fields, hauling crops to town and moving livestock from summer pastures to their winter homes.

But this harvest season, they’re doing it with diesel prices more than $2.50 per gallon higher than a year ago, adding to financial pressures from rising costs, unpredictable markets and shrinking profits.

“It seems like it’s coming at us from all directions,” said Brunkow, president of the Kansas Farm Bureau.

The economic strain is becoming a growing political concern for Republicans in states they have long dominated. President Donald Trump appeared in Kansas on Monday and will go to Iowa later in the week, the latest in a series of stops where he’s trying to energize his base in the final weeks before the midterm elections.

“In this election, I’m asking you to pretend please that I’m on the ballot,” Trump told the Kansas crowd. He spoke for over an hour and a half, with protesters interrupting him several times.

The visits come as Republicans pour money into Senate races in Kansas, Nebraska and Iowa amid concerns about voter enthusiasm. The anxiety may be especially notable in Kansas — a state Trump won by 16 percentage points against Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024 — as Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces a tough challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton. Democrats have not won a Senate election in Kansas in 94 years.

Hamilton, the founder of the nation’s largest United Methodist church, has attracted Republican support in his Senate bid, including endorsements from two former GOP governors. In a video statement ahead of Trump’s visit, Hamilton said it was “an honor” to welcome a sitting president to Kansas.

“I want Kansans to know that if you voted for the president, you also have a place in my campaign,” he added.

Brunkow, whose organization endorsed Marshall, said he’s been asked many times whether the economic frustrations could drive Republican farmers to vote for Democrats.

“I don’t think it necessarily does that,” Brunkow said. “But I think it dampens the enthusiasm for agriculture producers to get to the polls.”

Republican voters’ frustrations with the party have deepened

Don Hineman, a western Kansas rancher and former Republican state House majority leader, said he’s seeing growing frustration among GOP voters beyond just farmers, including some who have supported Trump in multiple elections.

He said farmers understand that Trump’s tariffs have hurt their businesses and are upset over the ongoing war with Iran. Immigration has also become a source of concern, particularly after recent immigration raids in western Kansas that resulted in the detention of more than 100 people.

“We need a secure border — we can all agree on that,” Hineman said. “But we also need workable immigration policy that provides the workforce that the United States has always depended on and will always continue to need.”

Hineman said the traditional Republican argument in Kansas — that electing Democrats would empower the party’s liberal wing — is losing its effectiveness with some voters, including himself.

“I am tired of being persuaded by charges that the boogeyman is going to get us,” he said. “I am so fed up with the Republican Party and their willingness to play sycophant to our current commander in chief that I’m willing to consider alternatives.”

Debbie Geneva, 61, of Nortonville, Kansas, said she was impressed by Hamilton after he visited a local market to meet people, something she hasn’t seen Marshall do. She’s never voted for a Democrat, she said, but remains undecided about the Senate race.

“I’ve never voted for a Democrat in my entire life, so that’s a little scary for me to be undecided,” said Geneva. “I told one of my friends that, and they can’t believe it, but that’s just the way I feel right now.”

Geneva said rising costs for healthcare and everyday expenses have added to her frustrations.

“And then of course the trade agreements,” she added. “The Republicans haven’t done the Midwest any favors with that.”

Farmers face a financial squeeze

Farmers have spent months feeling the squeeze as costs for inputs like diesel, fertilizer and seed have soared due to refinery constraints and supply disruptions tied to the Iran war.

Diesel averaged $6.30 per gallon nationwide on Friday, more than 70% higher than a year ago, according to motor club AAA. The surge has been especially painful during harvest season, when farmers depend heavily on fuel to operate machinery and transport crops.

“This is a time of year when we use a lot of fuel, and there just isn’t much we can do,” Brunkow said. “The margins are tight, and anything that cuts into that margin really hurts.”

The U.S. Department of Agriculture projects that net farm income will decline by 2.6% this year as production expenses rise by 4.5%. Fuel and oil expenses alone are expected to jump nearly 30%, according to the agency’s September forecast.

Trump said Monday night that the Department of Agriculture will be launching a new harvest fuel relief program, claiming it will provide $8 billion in support for farmers to offset diesel costs.

“When Republicans win, we will pass even more funding for our farmers. We love our farmers,” Trump said.

Earlier this month, Trump signed an executive order to ease limits on the tax-free use of red-dyed diesel, a decision he said would save “millions” for farmers. That came after a $12 billion aid package for farmers announced by the Trump administration in December.

But those efforts have not erased frustrations among some farmers who expected their financial outlook to improve under Trump.

Brunkow said many farmers “thought it would be better” under Trump.

“He’s made some unforced errors,” said Brunkow.

Concerns spread beyond Kansas

Trump will travel on Thursday to Iowa, where Republicans are defending competitive races for governor and Senate. The state, which Trump has carried in three consecutive presidential elections, is another agricultural stronghold where economic frustrations have become part of the political debate.

In Nebraska, Senate Republicans have poured nearly $15 million into a race between GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts and independent candidate Dan Osborn, an unprecedented amount for a state Trump won by 20 percentage points in 2024.

David McIntosh, president of the influential Club for Growth, said his group has kept a close eye on the heavy agriculture states since summer and acknowledged concerns about a drop-off in enthusiasm. His group is spending millions of dollars for GOP candidates in Kansas, Nebraska and elsewhere.

“Farmers are squeezed between higher input prices and less of an international market because of retaliatory tariffs,” McIntosh said. “The economic environment has not been good.”

Democrats, meanwhile, see an opportunity in the economic frustrations, even in states where they have struggled to win statewide elections.

Former Sen. Jon Tester, a Montana Democrat who lost reelection in 2024, said there is “no doubt” that Democrats will perform better than expected in agricultural states.

“These guys got to pay bills at the end of the month, and for a number of months now it’s been hard to do,” said Tester. “This is way beyond politics.”

news.title: Midlife women are using menopause as an identity – that's a disaster
news.text:
Somewhere along the line, menopause stopped being a stage of life and became an identity. No one is quite sure of the exact moment this happened, but it was at some point between Davina McCall’s 2021 landmark documentary and Boots selling vibrators to menopausal women online.

Menopause is no longer simply a hormonal shift expected in middle age – now it comes with a tote bag and a snazzy T-shirt that says “cougar puberty”. As well as hormone replacement therapy (HRT), there are menopause podcasts, menopause books, and menopause retreats. You can go down Tesco and buy cooling pyjamas, thermal comforters, and enough magnesium to tranquilise a small horse. Menopause culture and menopause products are everywhere.

After thousands of years of enduring symptoms in silence, women are now finally reclaiming the conversation and shouting openly, “I am hormonal and it f**king sucks!” And quite right too.

But there is a danger in turning menopause and perimenopause into identities rather than understanding them as experiences. We may be accidentally reviving the very prejudices and stereotypes we thought we were dismantling – namely, that women are slaves to their hormones, psychologically fragile, and overly emotional.

This matters because for most of our shared history, women have been viewed as the “weaker” sex precisely because of their biology. It was the ancient Greeks who first came up with the idea that women were ruled by their wombs and their emotions, and we have been fighting the repercussions of that ever since. We were too emotional to have the vote, too delicate to work, and too unstable to lead.

If you think such outdated opinions have been consigned to the historical dustbin, think again. According to one 2019 study, one in eight Americans think women are too emotional to rule, a fact we saw play out in the failed election bids of both Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris. Both women were widely attacked in the right-wing press as being “hysterical” or “unhinged” at various points in their campaigns. Research consistently shows us that women being unable to control their emotions is one of the oldest and most pernicious stereotypes in Western culture.

Yet here we are once again, willing to ascribe every wayward emotion, impulse, and irrationality in middle age to the almighty menopause. “Oh, I’m just menopausing” has become a common refrain amongst middle-aged women who may have forgotten what they walked into a room for. I’ve heard women apologise for being late and blame it on “peri-brain”. I have friends who have been rightly raging about an injustice at work but then check themselves by ascribing this emotion to a drop in oestrogen.

Aches, pains, and bad moods are now no longer simply because we are getting older and lead hectic lives – no, it’s because we are menopausal. All of which is reinforced by the proliferation of bullshit menopause products that have now swamped the market, telling us that our bodies and brains have gone insane and now require specialist care.

What we are seeing is the effacing of generic events that happen to all of us as we age, and the formation of an identity around the menopause that goes way beyond the symptoms initially being described. It is no longer something that is happening to you, but who you are – and the ongoing narrative around menopause tells us that person (read: woman) is emotional, unreliable, and liable to become periodically deranged. 

You can see this identity being formed in the funny T-shirts, the stand-up routines, the plotlines on telly, and just how quick we now are to chalk up every emotion a middle-aged woman experiences to the horrors of the menopause.

Identities can be powerful things as they bring a sense of belonging and can give context to what we experience. For someone in the throes of menopause, knowing you are not alone can be transformational. But identities are also dangerous, as people tend to react badly when theirs are challenged and often start to filter all their experiences through the identity prism. The effects of the menopause then become a self-fulfilling prophecy: women are now expecting the mood swings, the forgetfulness, the irritability, and the stiffening joints, and so assume the mantle of menopausal instability as soon as the first hot flush hits.

There is a delicate balance to be struck here. The symptoms of fluctuating hormone levels that accompany perimenopause and menopause are not an identity, they are real. Anxiety, depression, insomnia, and hot flushes are potentially debilitating and require proper medical attention. Employers should take this seriously, doctors should listen, and real treatment should be accessible. But we can acknowledge the biological changes without surrendering the person.

I worry that in the rush to finally name what is happening when hormones start to shift, we are playing into the ancient misogynistic trope that women are at the mercy of their reproductive systems and ultimately are overly emotional, constitutionally weak, and not in control.

A woman can experience a profound change in her body without becoming a cautionary tale about female irrationality. She can be both angry and right, tired but ambitious, and teary but competent.

We don’t need specialist skincare, diets, clothing, supplements, workout routines, and vibrators during menopause and perimenopause. Diminishing oestrogen does not turn us in to weak, delicate little flowers who have lost the run of themselves. What we need is accessible treatment, more research, and support from those around us when required. 

We can’t pretend that hormonal changes have no effect – they most certainly do. But a diagnosis can explain why someone has been struggling without redefining who they are.

news.title: Susan Collins Could Be Saved by Kamala Harris Voters
news.text: Republican Senator Susan Collins’ chances of defeating Democratic challenger Troy Jackson in the Maine Senate race could hinge on voters who supported her in the past but also backed former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024. These ticket-splitters could be decisive in the Maine Senate race, which has emerged as one of the handful of Senate races that could determine whether Democrats or Republicans win control of the Senate in the November 3 elections. Polling points to a close race in the Pine Tree State. Although Maine generally leans toward Democrats, Collins has been able to win reelection in the past due to her personal popularity and moderate image. But Democrats believe she may be vulnerable this year, as President Donald Trump’s unpopularity fuels a more challenging national environment for the GOP. Collins is an anomaly in the Senate, being the only Republican representing a state won by Harris in the 2024 election. In fact, she is the only senator from either party representing a state that has consistently voted against her party on the presidential level. The electorate is expected to be even bluer this year. Historically, midterm turnout is generally higher among the party not in the White House. These midterm dynamics and the partisan lean of Maine mean Collins must win a significant number of Harris voters this year. A key group to watch will be pro-choice women, who have supported Collins in the past but may be less willing to do so following her vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who voted to overturn Roe v. Wade, James Melcher, professor of political science at the University of Maine at Farmington, told Newsweek. “2020 cut Collins’ margin from 2014 from a 30+ point win to 9 points. This race will look far more like 2020 than 2014. Collins lost a lot of Democrats and independents,” he said. Newsweek reached out to the Collins and Jackson campaigns for comment via email. Maine Senate Race Could Rest on Ticket Splitters Ticket splitters are going to be a powerful force in Maine this year. Collins will have to win some voters who are also backing Democrat Hannah Pingree in the gubernatorial race. Polling suggests Pingree is a heavy favorite to win the race against Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett. Mark Brewer, a professor of political science at the University of Maine in Orono, told Newsweek these ticket splitters are likely to be moderates from both parties “who are turned off by both DSA and MAGA types.” These voters could be swayed on “competence” and an “ability to get things done,” he added. “Jackson would need to be able to make the case for his accomplishments in Maine state government, which he hasn't spent much time doing thus far,” Brewer said. Independents and Women: Maine Ticket Splitters Who Could Decide Election Polling suggests that while partisan voters are voting for their party and independents are in play in this year’s Senate race. While independents are closely divided in the Senate race, Pingree is winning them by a comfortable margin in the three-way gubernatorial race. In a recent YouGov/CBS News poll, Jackson led independent voters by 7 points, 53 percent to 46 percent, while Pingree held a 19-point lead among independents, 59 percent to 40 percent. A survey from Suffolk University gave Collins a 3-point lead among independents, 47 percent to 44 percent. But at the same time, Pingree held a large lead with 47 percent to Charles’ 32 percent and Bennett’s 13 percent. The Suffolk poll surveyed 500 Maine voters from October 8 to 11 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points, while the YouGov/CBS poll surveyed 1,144 registered voters from September 23 to October 1, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.7 percentage points. Women are also going to be an important voting bloc in the election. In 2020, when Collins last won reelection, she won women by 3 points, 49 percent to 46 percent over Democrat Sara Gideon, according to CNN exit polling data. At the same time, former President Joe Biden won women by more than 20 points, 61 percent to 38 percent, against Trump. Exit polling data for Maine in the 2024 election is not available. Polling suggests Collins is losing women to Jackson but still outperforming other Republicans. A critical question facing her campaign in the final weeks is whether she can lock up support from undecided moderate women who usually vote for Democrats, but have also voted for her in the past. The Suffolk poll found Collins trailing Jackson by 7 points among women, 52 percent to 43 percent, but Pingree led women by 17 points, 52 percent to 35 percent. The YouGov poll showed Jackson up 10 points among women, 55 percent to 45 percent, while Pingree led by 23 points, 61 percent to 38 percent. What Latest Polls Show About the Maine Senate Race Polling suggests the Maine Senate race will be one of the most competitive of the midterms. The Suffolk poll gave Jackson a 2-point lead, 49 percent to 47 percent, while the two were tied in the YouGov/CBS poll, each receiving support from 50 percent of respondents. Jackson led by 4 points in another recent poll from The Washington Post and George Mason University, conducted among 800 likely voters from September 30 to October 5. It found Jackson with 50 percent support, while 46 percent of respondents said they would vote for Collins. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. However, polling underestimated Collins in her 2020 reelection bid. She trailed Democrat Sara Gideon in most surveys but went on to win her reelection with a slim majority of the vote. Polling errors are not necessarily repeated from cycle-to-cycle, but whether a similar miss will occur this year remains a question hanging over the campaign. Forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball classify the race as a toss-up. Why the Maine Senate Race Matters in the 2026 Midterms The Maine Senate race has national implications. Currently, Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate, so Democrats must flip four seats to win control of the chamber, as Vice President JD Vance would serve as tiebreaker in a tie. Maine is seen as one of Democrats’ top pick up opportunities to flip a GOP-held seat given the state’s Democratic lean and the overall national environment favoring Democrats. Failing to flip Maine would narrow Democrats’ path to a Senate majority. They would have to make up for that loss in a double-digit Trump seat, which would be seen as a tougher lift. What Prediction Markets Show Jackson was narrowly ahead of Collins in prediction markets on Monday, having a 62 percent chance of winning on Kalshi and a 63 percent chance on Polymarket. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always predict the future accurately. Maine Senate Race: Latest Developments Collins and Jackson faced off last week in the final two debates in Maine. The final debate was briefly interrupted by a data center protester as Collins was speaking, to which the Republican senator said, “This is obviously one of Troy’s supporters.” Jackson responded, “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.” Jackson’s remark drew some criticism from Collins. Jackson declined to apologize during an interview on CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday. “I’ve had four debates with Senator Collins. I’ve shook her hand afterwards every time. What I’m not going to be is talked down to by Senator Collins, I’m not going to be accused of things like that. I’m fighting for Mainers and I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me so I’m not going to apologize for that,” he said. Last week, Jackson’s campaign filed its first financial disclosure form with the Federal Election Commission (FEC), which showed that Jackson outraised Collins four-to-one in the most recent quarter, though he remains behind in overall fundraising and outside assistance. Former President Barack Obama recently endorsed Jackson, while Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, traveled to the state to campaign with him over the weekend. Trump has also floated the idea of visiting Maine ahead of the midterms in remarks to reporters, though Collins said during an earlier debate she does not believe the president will visit the state. "I’ve heard nothing from his office, and I’m not exactly his favorite senator," she said. "I would say that he is not coming to Maine." Maine Voting: What to Know In-person absentee voting began on October 5 and will continue until October 29, according to the Maine secretary of state’s office. More than 70,000 Mainers had requested an absentee ballot as of October 2, according to the office. Polling locations are open between 6 a.m. or 10 a.m. to 8 p.m., depending on a town’s population, according to the secretary of state’s office. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Anthony Murray and Jason Lemon.
news.summary: Collins, the only GOP senator in a state Trump lost three times, is an anomaly. Her reelection depends on winning Harris voters.

news.title: After years of backlash, Apu returns to 'The Simpsons' with a South Asian voice
news.text: Across 38 seasons of “The Simpsons,” the Halloween-themed “Treehouse of Horror” episodes have always been a treat of spooky stand-alone storylines. On Sunday, the show surprised viewers with a major resurrection: Apu, the beloved Kwik-E-Mart operator who had not been heard for the better part of a decade, spoke once again in Springfield.He and his wife, Manjula, were back with a meaty plotline — and the voices of actual Indian American actors: Sunil Malhotra, a veteran voice-over artist, and Janina Gavankar (“The Morning Show”).“Bringing Apu back feels like a reclamation. It truly IS his homecoming,” Malhotra and Gavankar said Sunday in a joint Instagram post.Apu's unheralded return is a remarkable twist to a yearslong discourse about how the character has represented a painful stereotype for some South Asian Americans. After a 2017 documentary by comedian Hari Kondabolu, “The Problem With Apu,” the character was largely exiled from the screen.How a documentary on Apu became a turning pointIn “The Problem With Apu,” Kondabolu, a self-described fan of the Fox show, tried to process his misgivings. He interviewed a slew of celebrities of South Asian origin, including Kal Penn, Utkarsh Ambudkar and Hasan Minhaj, about growing up with the character. They shared memories of being bullied and called “Apu” as an insult. Adding to their view of Apu as just a caricature was that Hank Azaria, a white actor, voiced him.With the full name of Apu Nahasapeemapetilon Jr., he felt like the “forever foreigner, someone who represents Indians in the United States through this sole typology of being a convenience store owner, being a recent immigrant, having this heavy accent, being really limited in this sort of like American identity,” says Bhoomi Thakore, an assistant professor of sociology at the University of Connecticut. Thakore notes that Kondabolu's film raised the notion that Apu was the only portrayal of an Indian character most people knew when he debuted in 1990.Azaria stepped away from the role after the documentary, continuing to voice other “Simpsons” characters, as Apu fell silent, seen only in the background. Kondabolu, however, had never called for Apu to be canceled. On Monday, he praised “The Simpsons” for devising “a clever solution to all this” and hiring Malhotra and Gavankar.“I’m also still proud of the public conversation about race and representation my documentary started,” he told The Associated Press in an emailed statement. “Finally, I’m hoping this stops all the hatemail in many languages that has been sent my way over the past decade.”After years in the background, Apu appears here to stayIn a 2018 episode, “The Simpsons” responded to Kondabolu's documentary by having Lisa Simpson bemoan how “something that started decades ago and was applauded and inoffensive is now politically incorrect. ... What can you do?” The camera then panned to a framed photo of Apu. The gag was branded by some as weak for not directly addressing the controversy.In a 2020 New York Times interview, Azaria, who by then hadn't voiced Apu in a few years, announced he would bow out because “it just didn't feel right.” Later that year, in response to racial reckoning demonstrations, “The Simpsons” announced it would no longer cast white voice actors as characters of color. The show then recast two Black characters, Carl Carlson and Dr. Julius Hibbert, with Black actors.Kondabolu had not spoken with “The Simpsons” producers about Apu’s comeback, he confirmed to the AP, “but they didn’t owe me that.” And it does sound like Apu is here to stay.“We love this character and wanted to bring him back in a smart, Simpsons-y way that allowed him to evolve,” executive producer Matt Selman said in a statement. “We’re excited by what Sunil has already brought to the role and look forward to seeing more of Apu in the future.”Apu was also embraced by South Asians, despite the controversyA few weeks after “The Simpsons” responded to the documentary, author and producer Amar Shah wrote a series of social media posts and then a Washington Post op-ed on why he felt mostly sentimental toward Apu. When he watched Apu, he thought of his own Indian father hard at work as a convenience store owner and how that shaped his Florida childhood.“Apu even now is a character that I wouldn't mind my kids seeing represented because they'll see aspects of themselves and of their own grandparents,” says Shah, reflecting on his 2018 piece. “I can totally empathize with someone of South Asian origin having a different POV (point of view) than me but this is my childhood. This is my story.”After watching this latest episode, Shah didn't sense any significant difference with Malhotra's performance.“Obviously, there's a different voice, tenor, texture and all that. But, the character is always going to be there, his genuine humanity,” Shah says. “I think if they had incorporated this change earlier, it would have been a lot better.”At a time of anti-South Asian hate, Apu's return is welcomedApu is being revived amid a climate of rising anti-South Asian and Indian hate. Stop AAPI Hate and other research groups have found online use of racist slurs and threats against South Asians and Indians have jumped in the past few years.Texas Railroad Commission candidate Bo French, a Republican, recently posted a photo of South Asian University of Texas students cheering at a football game and called them “a problem.” Just last week, a man was charged with planning a mass shooting at a Hindu temple outside Chicago. Against that backdrop, Shah welcomes the show's careful approach reincarnating the character.“It's great to see that the show has evolved in time and now, especially with the discrimination and, really, the targeting of South Asians and Indian Americans as of late — questioning our patriotism, our American identity and even whether we're college football fans,” he says.The return also coincides with much more representation of prominent South Asian Americans, such as actor and showrunner Mindy Kaling, and people who have broken barriers in office, like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and former Vice President Kamala Harris.When Apu first appeared, says University of Virginia associate professor of media studies Shilpa Davé, he was one of the only consistent representations of South Asians on TV.Now, she says, “South Asians have become a part of the landscape from ‘Bridgerton’ to … ‘Never Have I Ever’ and there’s a plethora of different kinds of representation.”

news.title: Vivek Ramaswamy in close race in Ohio against Democrat Amy Acton
news.text:
Washington: Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is in a neck-and-neck battle with Democrat Amy Acton in the gubernatorial race in Ohio, with a latest opinion poll giving the Indian-American entrepreneur a slender three-point lead over his rival.

Endorsed by US President Donald Trump last year, 41-year-old Ramaswamy entered the election for Ohio Governor as a clear favourite but is now facing a tough challenge from Acton, the former state health chief.

If Ramaswamy wins the November 3 election, he will become the third person of Indian descent to hold a gubernatorial post after Bobby Jindal in Louisiana and Nikki Haley in South Carolina.

However, the biotech billionaire has had a tough campaign, and his attempt to reach out to college students in Ohio ended in disaster in July when he was forced off stage by a right-wing crowd over his “winners versus whiners” speech.

“Are you in the camp of people in this country who want to win? Or are you in the camp of people who want to whine?” he asked a young crowd, which responded with boos and heckling and forced him to “peace out”.

news.title: After years of backlash, Apu returns to 'The Simpsons' with a South Asian voice
news.text: Across 38 seasons of “The Simpsons,” the Halloween-themed “Treehouse of Horror” episodes have always been a treat of spooky stand-alone storylines. On Sunday, the show surprised viewers with a major resurrection: Apu, the beloved Kwik-E-Mart operator who had not been heard for the better part of a decade, spoke once again in Springfield. He and his wife, Manjula, were back with a meaty plotline — and the voices of actual Indian American actors: Sunil Malhotra, a veteran voice-over artist, and Janina Gavankar (“The Morning Show”). “Bringing Apu back feels like a reclamation. It truly IS his homecoming,” Malhotra and Gavankar said Sunday in a joint Instagram post. Apu's unheralded return is a remarkable twist to a yearslong discourse about how the character has represented a painful stereotype for some South Asian Americans. After a 2017 documentary by comedian Hari Kondabolu, “The Problem With Apu,” the character was largely exiled from the screen. How a documentary on Apu became a turning point In “The Problem With Apu,” Kondabolu, a self-described fan of the Fox show, tried to process his misgivings. He interviewed a slew of celebrities of South Asian origin, including Kal Penn, Utkarsh Ambudkar and Hasan Minhaj, about growing up with the character. They shared memories of being bullied and called “Apu” as an insult. Adding to their view of Apu as just a caricature was that Hank Azaria, a white actor, voiced him. With the full name of Apu Nahasapeemapetilon Jr., he felt like the “forever foreigner, someone who represents Indians in the United States through this sole typology of being a convenience store owner, being a recent immigrant, having this heavy accent, being really limited in this sort of like American identity,” says Bhoomi Thakore, an assistant professor of sociology at the University of Connecticut. Thakore notes that Kondabolu's film raised the notion that Apu was the only portrayal of an Indian character most people knew when he debuted in 1990. Azaria stepped away from the role after the documentary, continuing to voice other “Simpsons” characters, as Apu fell silent, seen only in the background. Kondabolu, however, had never called for Apu to be canceled. On Monday, he praised “The Simpsons” for devising “a clever solution to all this” and hiring Malhotra and Gavankar. “I’m also still proud of the public conversation about race and representation my documentary started,” he told The Associated Press in an emailed statement. “Finally, I’m hoping this stops all the hatemail in many languages that has been sent my way over the past decade.” After years in the background, Apu appears here to stay In a 2018 episode, “The Simpsons” responded to Kondabolu's documentary by having Lisa Simpson bemoan how “something that started decades ago and was applauded and inoffensive is now politically incorrect. ... What can you do?” The camera then panned to a framed photo of Apu. The gag was branded by some as weak for not directly addressing the controversy. In a 2020 New York Times interview, Azaria, who by then hadn't voiced Apu in a few years, announced he would bow out because “it just didn't feel right.” Later that year, in response to racial reckoning demonstrations, “The Simpsons” announced it would no longer cast white voice actors as characters of color. The show then recast two Black characters, Carl Carlson and Dr. Julius Hibbert, with Black actors. Kondabolu had not spoken with “The Simpsons” producers about Apu’s comeback, he confirmed to the AP, “but they didn’t owe me that.” And it does sound like Apu is here to stay. “We love this character and wanted to bring him back in a smart, Simpsons-y way that allowed him to evolve,” executive producer Matt Selman said in a statement. “We’re excited by what Sunil has already brought to the role and look forward to seeing more of Apu in the future.” Apu was also embraced by South Asians, despite the controversy A few weeks after “The Simpsons” responded to the documentary, author and producer Amar Shah wrote a series of social media posts and then a Washington Post op-ed on why he felt mostly sentimental toward Apu. When he watched Apu, he thought of his own Indian father hard at work as a convenience store owner and how that shaped his Florida childhood. “Apu even now is a character that I wouldn't mind my kids seeing represented because they'll see aspects of themselves and of their own grandparents,” says Shah, reflecting on his 2018 piece. “I can totally empathize with someone of South Asian origin having a different POV [point of view] than me but this is my childhood. This is my story.” After watching this latest episode, Shah didn't sense any significant difference with Malhotra's performance. “Obviously, there's a different voice, tenor, texture and all that. But, the character is always going to be there, his genuine humanity,” Shah says. “I think if they had incorporated this change earlier, it would have been a lot better.” At a time of anti-South Asian hate, Apu's return is welcomed Apu is being revived amid a climate of rising anti-South Asian and Indian hate. Stop AAPI Hate and other research groups have found online use of racist slurs and threats against South Asians and Indians have jumped in the past few years. Texas Railroad Commission candidate Bo French, a Republican, recently posted a photo of South Asian University of Texas students cheering at a football game and called them “a problem.” Just last week, a man was charged with planning a mass shooting at a Hindu temple outside Chicago. Against that backdrop, Shah welcomes the show's careful approach reincarnating the character. “It's great to see that the show has evolved in time and now, especially with the discrimination and, really, the targeting of South Asians and Indian Americans as of late — questioning our patriotism, our American identity and even whether we're college football fans,” he says. The return also coincides with much more representation of prominent South Asian Americans, such as actor and showrunner Mindy Kaling, and people who have broken barriers in office, like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and former Vice President Kamala Harris. When Apu first appeared, says University of Virginia associate professor of media studies Shilpa Davé, he was one of the only consistent representations of South Asians on TV. Now, she says, “South Asians have become a part of the landscape from ‘Bridgerton’ to … ‘Never Have I Ever’ and there’s a plethora of different kinds of representation.”

news.title: As Election Day Nears, Trump Promises Additional $8 Billion To Farmers
news.text:
TOPEKA, Kan. (AP) — Fifth-generation Kansas farmer Glenn Brunkow describes this time of year as “go time,” when farmers are combining fields, hauling crops to town and moving livestock from summer pastures to their winter homes.

But this harvest season, they’re doing it with diesel prices more than $2.50 per gallon higher than a year ago, adding to financial pressures from rising costs, unpredictable markets and shrinking profits.

“It seems like it’s coming at us from all directions,” said Brunkow, president of the Kansas Farm Bureau.

The economic strain is becoming a growing political concern for Republicans in states they have long dominated. President Donald Trump appeared in Kansas on Monday and will go to Iowa later in the week, the latest in a series of stops where he’s trying to energize his base in the final weeks before the midterm elections.

“In this election, I’m asking you to pretend please that I’m on the ballot,” Trump told the Kansas crowd. He spoke for over an hour and a half, with protesters interrupting him several times.

The visits come as Republicans pour money into Senate races in Kansas, Nebraska and Iowa amid concerns about voter enthusiasm. The anxiety may be especially notable in Kansas — a state Trump won by 16 percentage points against Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024 — as Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces a tough challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton. Democrats have not won a Senate election in Kansas in 94 years.

Hamilton, the founder of the nation’s largest United Methodist church, has attracted Republican support in his Senate bid, including endorsements from two former GOP governors. In a video statement ahead of Trump’s visit, Hamilton said it was “an honor” to welcome a sitting president to Kansas.

“I want Kansans to know that if you voted for the president, you also have a place in my campaign,” he added.

Brunkow, whose organization endorsed Marshall, said he’s been asked many times whether the economic frustrations could drive Republican farmers to vote for Democrats.

“I don’t think it necessarily does that,” Brunkow said. “But I think it dampens the enthusiasm for agriculture producers to get to the polls.”

Republican voters’ frustrations with the party have deepened

Don Hineman, a western Kansas rancher and former Republican state House majority leader, said he’s seeing growing frustration among GOP voters beyond just farmers, including some who have supported Trump in multiple elections.

He said farmers understand that Trump’s tariffs have hurt their businesses and are upset over the ongoing war with Iran. Immigration has also become a source of concern, particularly after recent immigration raids in western Kansas that resulted in the detention of more than 100 people.

“We need a secure border — we can all agree on that,” Hineman said. “But we also need workable immigration policy that provides the workforce that the United States has always depended on and will always continue to need.”

Hineman said the traditional Republican argument in Kansas — that electing Democrats would empower the party’s liberal wing — is losing its effectiveness with some voters, including himself.

“I am tired of being persuaded by charges that the boogeyman is going to get us,” he said. “I am so fed up with the Republican Party and their willingness to play sycophant to our current commander in chief that I’m willing to consider alternatives.”

Debbie Geneva, 61, of Nortonville, Kansas, said she was impressed by Hamilton after he visited a local market to meet people, something she hasn’t seen Marshall do. She’s never voted for a Democrat, she said, but remains undecided about the Senate race.

“I’ve never voted for a Democrat in my entire life, so that’s a little scary for me to be undecided,” said Geneva. “I told one of my friends that, and they can’t believe it, but that’s just the way I feel right now.”

Geneva said rising costs for healthcare and everyday expenses have added to her frustrations.

“And then of course the trade agreements,” she added. “The Republicans haven’t done the Midwest any favors with that.”

Farmers face a financial squeeze

Farmers have spent months feeling the squeeze as costs for inputs like diesel, fertilizer and seed have soared due to refinery constraints and supply disruptions tied to the Iran war.

Diesel averaged $6.30 per gallon nationwide on Friday, more than 70% higher than a year ago, according to motor club AAA. The surge has been especially painful during harvest season, when farmers depend heavily on fuel to operate machinery and transport crops.

“This is a time of year when we use a lot of fuel, and there just isn’t much we can do,” Brunkow said. “The margins are tight, and anything that cuts into that margin really hurts.”

The U.S. Department of Agriculture projects that net farm income will decline by 2.6% this year as production expenses rise by 4.5%. Fuel and oil expenses alone are expected to jump nearly 30%, according to the agency’s September forecast.

Trump said Monday night that the Department of Agriculture will be launching a new harvest fuel relief program, claiming it will provide $8 billion in support for farmers to offset diesel costs.

“When Republicans win, we will pass even more funding for our farmers. We love our farmers,” Trump said.

Earlier this month, Trump signed an executive order to ease limits on the tax-free use of red-dyed diesel, a decision he said would save “millions” for farmers. That came after a $12 billion aid package for farmers announced by the Trump administration in December.

But those efforts have not erased frustrations among some farmers who expected their financial outlook to improve under Trump.

Brunkow said many farmers “thought it would be better” under Trump.

“He’s made some unforced errors,” said Brunkow.

Concerns spread beyond Kansas

Trump will travel on Thursday to Iowa, where Republicans are defending competitive races for governor and Senate. The state, which Trump has carried in three consecutive presidential elections, is another agricultural stronghold where economic frustrations have become part of the political debate.

In Nebraska, Senate Republicans have poured nearly $15 million into a race between GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts and independent candidate Dan Osborn, an unprecedented amount for a state Trump won by 20 percentage points in 2024.

David McIntosh, president of the influential Club for Growth, said his group has kept a close eye on the heavy agriculture states since summer and acknowledged concerns about a drop-off in enthusiasm. His group is spending millions of dollars for GOP candidates in Kansas, Nebraska and elsewhere.

“Farmers are squeezed between higher input prices and less of an international market because of retaliatory tariffs,” McIntosh said. “The economic environment has not been good.”

Democrats, meanwhile, see an opportunity in the economic frustrations, even in states where they have struggled to win statewide elections.

Former Sen. Jon Tester, a Montana Democrat who lost reelection in 2024, said there is “no doubt” that Democrats will perform better than expected in agricultural states.

“These guys got to pay bills at the end of the month, and for a number of months now it’s been hard to do,” said Tester. “This is way beyond politics.”

Cappelletti reported from Washington. Associated Press journalists Nick Ingram and Collin Binkley contributed to this report.

news.title: In ruby-red Kansas, Trump contemplates the possibility of a Democratic win in the state
news.text:
The fact that Donald Trump was here at all said more about a looming electoral disaster facing his Republican party next month than anything contained in his dark and discursive 98-minute stump speech.

On Monday, amid raucous chants of “USA! USA!”, the president held his first campaign rally in Kansas for eight years. No Democrat has won a US Senate seat in this ruby-red state since 1932, the year Herbert Hoover was president, Amelia Earhart was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic and the Nazis became the biggest party in the German Reichstag.

Since then Republicans in the state have built one of the longest winning streaks in Senate history, but such is the collapse in public esteem of the president that the midterms on 3 November could be the night that a blue wave engulfs the heart of Trump country.

“You’re really sort of – I hate to say it – you’re sort of tending toward the purple,” the president told about 5,000 supporters in a multipurpose arena outside Wichita, acknowledging that Kansas already has a Democratic governor in Laura Kelly. “That’s why I have to be sure that we get this guy.”

The “guy” concerned was Roger Marshall, a first-term Republican senator facing an unexpectedly strong challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor. Opinion polls show them running neck and neck. In the third quarter, Hamilton reportedly raised $11m while Marshall managed just $800,000.

Marshall, 66, is an obstetrician-gynaecologist and ex-congressman who has proved a staunch Trump ally, including by embracing his debunked claim that the 2020 presidential election was stolen. Hamilton, 62, founded the 24,000-member Church of the Resurrection, the biggest United Methodist congregation in the country. He opposes Trump’s tariff agenda and what he calls the president’s “erratic leadership”.

Despite Hamilton’s background as a pastor and former Republican, Marshall insisted on Monday that Hamilton was “too woke for Kansas”. Accompanied by Chuck Berry’s Johnny B Goode as he walked on stage, Marshall said: “This is a guy that participates in protests against police. He supports drag shows. He tells us to apologise for the colour of our skin. And in a state with more cattle than people, he tells you to stop eating beef.” The crowd jeered each time.

Trump, 80, is barnstorming the country in what some have called a “desperation tour” aimed at rescuing Republicans from the hole he has dug for them. Critics suggest he might actually be making life harder by nationalising races that candidates would prefer to keep focused on local issues.

By imposing himself in Kansas, at a rally that was disrupted by several protesters, Trump underlined the election as a referendum on his presidency, with the potential to cost Republicans control of both the Senate and House of Representatives just two years after they swept into power.

Farmers in Kansas, a heavily agricultural state, have been hit hard by the consequences of the Iran war: a gallon of diesel costs nearly $6. The president upset cattle ranchers with a plan to reduce import tariffs to lower the price of beef and with aggressive immigration raids that prompted some agricultural workers to stay at home. On Monday Trump announced a new program to provide farmers with $8bn in support to offset diesel costs during the harvest season.

The election will test whether the old playbooks that fuelled his presidential campaigns – hurling insults, stirring bigotry and telling lies – can still work among an electorate weary of the cost of living, foreign wars and government corruption.

Trump launched a tirade against Hamilton, dismissing him as a “radical left lunatic” and a “phoney who’s pretending to be a moderate”. Trump claimed the Democrat supports flooding Kansas with refugees who “go around killing people”, that he used church money to fund “transgender crap”, that he “openly mocks Jesus” and that he believes America is systemically racist.

“He wants you to repent for being born white,” Trump said.

The president also sought to weaponise the recent upheaval in France, pushing the baseless nativist claim that the violence is being led by immigrants. “We’re not going to let that happen to this country,” he said. “When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to ​do to America.”

Trump unleashed bitter attacks on three Muslim politicians: Abdul El-Sayed, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib. When Tlaib’s name was mentioned, members of the crowd yelled: “Deport her!” Trump falsely claimed that both El-Sayed and his sister are members of the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist opposition group in Egypt. He mockingly warned that, should El-Sayed be elected and sit on the Senate intelligence committee, he would leak information to the enemy.

Supporters roared their approved, thrilled by what they saw as Trump’s transgressive daring. The president, who won Kansas by 16 percentage points against Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024, showed he can still draw a crowd in one of the most surprising battleground states in the country.

Earlier, in warm sunshine, a long line of people snaked through fields outside the arena. There were sights that have become familiar over more than a decade: giant Trump flags, tables full of “Make America great again” caps, spangly “DJT” and “Trump the golden age” jackets, “Alligator Alcatraz” merchandise, “We are all Charlie Kirk now” sweaters and T-shirts that said “Stand for the flag, kneel for the cross”.

One woman wore a sweater that said: “0% liberal.” One man wore a T-shirt that declared: “I love Trump because he pisses off all the people I can’t stand.”

For these supporters, Trump rallies are galvanising and still the best way to get out the Republican vote. Cybersecurity worker Justin Nelsen, 44, said: “It fires us up, it gets us all excited for the cause and allows us to put out there what we want here as the state of Kansas. That’s why I’m here.”

Attendees were aware of the danger posed by Hamilton. Brittany Jones, a 33-year-old lawyer wearing a Stars and Stripes sweater, said: “If you know Adam Hamilton at all you know that he’s a problem and a chameleon and good at saying what he thinks people want to hear, even if he doesn’t believe it. He has shown himself to be not only a turncoat to things that matter to Christians, he has wholly given himself to the local agenda. Even though he claims to be a moderate, there’s nothing moderate about him.”

A Democratic victory here would represent a political earthquake, Jones acknowledged. “It’s seismic. It would be sad for most Kansans when they realise what happened, and some people just aren’t thinking through the consequences, but he has a built-in audience of people who are highly motivated.”

Jones, who had her friend’s three-month-old baby, Hannah, tucked under one arm, said she mostly welcomed Trump’s second term. “Overall I care about the social issues and he’s done a lot to protect girls’ sports, he’s done a lot to protect kids from being put through harmful gender transition procedures. Those things matter to me, they matter to the future of girls all across Kansas and America, and so I’m excited about those things.”

Construction worker Thad Snider, 42, who attended wearing a red “Make America Great Again” T-shirt alongside his mother, said he was not overly worried about the Senate seat falling to the Democrats.

“I don’t think Adam’s as strong a candidate as what the media is trying to sell him as,” he said, pointing to Hamilton’s past political donations to Democrats including Hillary Clinton. “I don’t think it’s going to happen but, if it did happen, it would be very shocking.”

Snider argues that voters faced a stark choice between political parties, describing the Republicans as the “least bad” option because “at least they’re not socialists or communists”. He added that he disagreed with foreign wars and wished Trump had done more on election integrity, but remained loyal to the president. “Any time you turn around a battleship, it takes time.”

That sentiment was echoed by Darrell Claphan, 72, a retired sales worker, who said of Trump: “He’s doing fantastic. He’ll go down in history being the number one president at what he’s done for the country in my lifetime.”

Claphan dismissed opinion polls showing a close race, stating: “Polls have been wrong ever since I’ve been alive.”

Asked how he would react to a Democratic Senate victory in Kansas, Claphan said: “I’d be shocked. But I don’t think it’s going to happen.”

news.title: New Mexico Republican Rejects Trump’s Push to Rename State
news.text: Gregg Hull, Republican candidate for governor in New Mexico, balked at President Donald Trump's push to rename the state as "New America." In a post to Truth Social earlier on Monday, the president said, "New Mexico should immediately change its name to New America. We are not Mexico, we are the United States of America!" He said the name change would add great "value and prestige," adding that incomes and home values would rise. "Maybe even the Crooked Elections, that New Mexico is known for, would become honest again!" Trump said. Hull responded to the president's idea in a post to X on Monday night, saying in part that he stands by his original statement that "New Mexico does not need a new name." This is not the first time the president has floated the idea. In September, he posted a picture depicting the state with Mexico crossed out and America written below. During his time in office, the president has also rebranded the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America and Lake Ontario to Lake America. He has also floated renaming the Strait of Hormuz as the "Trump Strait" amid the country's ongoing war with Iran. When reached about Hull's remarks, the White House referred Newsweek to the president's comments. What To Know Hull added in his post on X that the state's identity is rooted in rich culture, beautiful landscape and the resilience of its people. "That identity is never up for negotiation. EVER," Hull said. He added that the people of New Mexico are focused on good-paying jobs, taxes and an economy that works for families, energy independence and relief from rising costs. "That is where my focus is, and that is what the campaign is about," Hull concluded. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Trump lost New Mexico during the 2024 presidential election to then-Vice President Kamala Harris by roughly 6 percent. Trump's overall approval rating and ranking on specific policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have slipped as households across America are consistently flagging affordability concerns. news.title: Top Dem Strategist Makes Shock Midterms Wish
news.text:
Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville has revealed his surprising take on how he’d like the midterms to pan out.

Carville, 81, told The Bulwark’s Bill Kristol that he would rather see Republicans keep the House majority by five seats than have Democrats take it by the same margin.

“I would be disappointed if it comes in at 225 House seats,” the former Bill Clinton aide told Kristol on the Bulwark on Sunday podcast. “That would almost be—I would rather the Republicans keep the House by five than the Democrats to win by five because if that happens, they’re hostage to the DSA.”

Carville was referring to the Democratic Socialists of America, a progressive wing of the Democratic Party that has surged in popularity over the last year and includes populist leaders like New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Carville said that only a slight majority would be difficult for Democratic House leaders, such as Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, to manage.

“Hakeem cannot move. There’s no place to go,” he said. “And even if you have a close Senate, Fetterman would keep Schumer Pepto-Bismol all night.”

“I think this one is one of these races where margin matters a lot,” the politico explained. “Winning big—it’s almost as big as winning, which is weird. But yeah, it’s a nightmare at 225.”

CNN’s Erin Burnett covered Carville’s remarks Monday night, asking former Fox News anchor Gretchen Carlson and former Kamala Harris aide Jamal Simmons their thoughts on his wish.

Carlson said she agreed with the veteran politico about the DSA being “problematic” for the Democratic Party, but disagreed that Democrats would want Republicans to keep the House.

Simmons, on the other hand, said most people in the mainstream Democratic Party don’t share Carville’s hardline views on the DSA.

“While there are lots of issues people may disagree with on the DSA, what they do want is somebody who’s gonna rip up the old playbook and do things differently,” he said. “The American public is interested in doing something really different.”

Carville has made his disdain for the rising democratic socialist coalition clear over the past several months.

After a string of DSA primary victories, such as Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania and Melat Kiros in Colorado, the strategist has unleashed criticism on the progressive splinter group, calling them “a bunch of silly people” and “a pack of fools.”

“Nobody pays attention to them. They don’t do anything,” he told Fox News’s Jesse Watters in August.

In June, he targeted New York DSA candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier directly, saying he doesn’t “have anything in common with someone that says they’re against interracial dating or doesn’t want any incarceration for convicted felons.”

He elevated his rhetoric in August, demanding that DSA candidates quit using the Democratic Party’s “goddamn name.”

news.title: Latino Support for GOP's Byron Donalds in Doubt for Florida Governor's Race
news.text: A new poll shows that Republican Byron Donalds leads Democrat David Jolly overall in the race to be Florida's next governor, but Latinos favor the Democrat by 5 percent. Donalds landed 50 percent overall compared to Jolly's 42 percent, the new N+ Univision/YouGov poll shows on Monday. Among Latinos however, Jolly received 48 percent compared to Donalds' 43 percent. The poll also shows that President Donald Trump's favorability among the key voting bloc is more negative versus the overall with 38 percent favorability compared to a 54 percent unfavorable rating. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Republicans now hold a narrow majority in both the House and Senate. Trump's overall approval rating and ranking on specific policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have slipped as households across America are consistently flagging affordability concerns. Trump won Florida, his home state, in the 2024 presidential election versus then-Vice President Kamala Harris by double digits. Winning the state was notable amid Trump's broader victory as he made inroads with Hispanic dominant communities and counties in the state like Miami-Dade, Hillsborough and Osceola. Newsweek reached out to both Jolly and Donalds' campaigns via email on Monday for comment. What To Know Florida, once considered a battleground, has shifted to the right over time and is now seen as a reliable pickup for Republicans. An influx of conservative retirees into the state, as well as Trump’s inroads with Latinos, helped turn the state into a stronghold. However, Democrats are hoping to make the state more competitive again in November's midterm with nominee Jolly for governor and Angie Nixon for U.S. Senate leading the top of the ticket. The new poll shows that Cubans favor Trump-endorsed Donalds by 51 percent to 42 percent, Puerto Ricans favor Jolly 51 percent to 35 percent and South Americans prefer Jolly 47 percent to Donalds' 44 percent. Among Latinos who voted for the president in 2024, 9 percent support Jolly, the poll shows. Fifty-five percent of Latinos also say that immigration enforcement has gone too far. That figure combines 32 percent who say the border needed securing, while noting that enforcement has gone too far and an additional 23 percent who say that the border situation was overstated, and enforcement has gone too far, according to the poll. The survey shows that 41 percent of Latinos are very or somewhat concerned that they or someone close to them could be affected by immigration enforcements. Twenty-nine percent of Latino Trump voters also say that immigration enforcement has gone too far, the poll shows. Affordability is a key issue among Sunshine State voters, and 59 percent of Latinos say jobs and the cost of living are a top issue in the state, 57 percent say the cost of housing and affordability while 33 percent say immigration and immigration enforcement. Clarissa Martinez, Vice President of Unidos US, a nonprofit and non-party affiliated organization, told Newsweek via email on Monday, “The poll is consistent with Hispanic voter sentiment in Florida and nationwide: there is widespread discontent with the economy. Hispanic voters have noted that the two top issues shaping Hispanic voters’ views of the President are the cost of living and immigration enforcement, and these are two potent factors swinging these voters away from Republicans.” The poll surveyed 825 Florida voters from October 2 to October 15 and had a margin of error of 4 percent. What Other Polling Shows A Stetson University Center for Public Opinion Research poll shows Donalds up 52 percent to Jolly's 41 percent among likely voters. The survey shows that about 5 percent are undecided and 3 percent would pick another candidate. The poll surveyed 826 Florida adults from October 1 to October 9 and had a 4.2 percent margin of error. A Mason-Dixon Poll for NBC 6 and Telemundo showed Donalds up 48 percent to Jolly's 41 percent overall. One percent said other and 10 percent were undecided. The poll surveyed 625 registered voters in the state from September 28 through October 1, 2026, with a margin of error of 4 percent. news.title: U.S. Supreme Court Ends Descendants' Fight Over Hastings Law School Name
news.text:
The U.S. Supreme Court has rejected a last-ditch challenge from descendants of Serranus C. Hastings, closing the book on a years-long legal fight over the removal of his name from San Francisco's 148-year-old law school. The justices denied review in Hastings College Conservation Committee v. State of California, case 25-1231, issuing a one-sentence order with no indication of dissents.

The dispute traces back to 2023, when the school formerly known as Hastings College of the Law became UC College of the Law, San Francisco, after the California Legislature passed Assembly Bill 1936. The San Francisco Chronicle reported that Assemblymember James Ramos sponsored the bill. According to the Los Angeles Times, Ramos — the first Native American elected to the state Assembly — introduced the measure, which was co-sponsored by Assemblymember Phil Ting and signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2022.

Six descendants of Hastings and a group of alumni sued California, accusing the state of violating a binding contract. The Chronicle's report notes the plaintiffs sought return of the original $100,000 gift plus interest, which they calculated at $1.7 million — though the Los Angeles Times reported a compounded demand of $1.7 billion, based on the original terms' 7% annual interest rate.

A Founder's Legacy Under Scrutiny

Serranus C. Hastings was California's first Chief Justice and later state Attorney General, in addition to being a rancher who committed $100,000 to establish the law school in 1878. California law at the time declared the school would forever be known as Hastings College of the Law. Per the Chronicle's reporting, Hastings blamed tribes for attacking his cattle and sent militia troops who killed Native Americans in Mendocino County, with the outlet reporting he ordered troops to slaughter thousands of Native Americans in the 1860s.

That history drew formal institutional scrutiny in 2017, when Chancellor David Faigman organized the Hastings Legacy Review Committee after a local op-ed detailed Hastings' history, according to CBS San Francisco. The committee's work culminated in a 2020 report documenting Hastings' role in financing the militia massacres, the station reported.

Courts Reject the Contract Claim

California courts repeatedly ruled the 1878 law was not a contract but an ordinary statute subject to repeal. Attorney Richard Ulmer said in 2024 that the original law authorized Hastings to found the college but did not require the state to keep his name attached permanently, according to the Chronicle's account. A California appeals court agreed that the 1878 law did not bind the state to preserve the name indefinitely, and the California Supreme Court subsequently left that ruling intact.

On October 15, 2025, California's First District Court of Appeal issued a unanimous decision authored by Justice Jeremy M. Goldman, holding that the state retained sovereign authority to manage and rename public institutions and that 19th-century statutory mandates do not bind future legislatures, per the USA Herald. The court rejected the plaintiffs' claims under the Contract Clause and prohibitions on bills of attainder. The state Supreme Court later denied a petition for review without comment, closing off state-level appeals before the case reached the nation's highest court.

Dueling Arguments From Both Sides

Attorney Gregory Michael, representing the plaintiffs through Dhillon Law Group, called the Supreme Court's decision disappointing and said the litigation sought to vindicate constitutional principles and preserve Judge Hastings' legacy against legislative action he believed exceeded constitutional limits. Michael denied that Hastings ordered mass killings of Native Americans, arguing instead that Hastings sought to deploy the militia to protect livestock and that the militia acted independently in committing atrocities. He told the court that allowing a state to tear up agreements after rewriting history by legislative decree renders constraints on state power meaningless, maintaining that California should remain bound by its 1878 agreement to name the school after Hastings.

Attorney Joshua Anderson countered that the law school could act after evidence was presented that Hastings funded and fomented genocide of Native Californians. Attorney Tara Siegel added that state legislatures may not bargain away their duties to regulate public matters. Law firm Cooley LLP represented the school's board of directors throughout the litigation.

Bill Kisliuk, a spokesperson for the law school, said officials welcomed the conclusion of the case and that UC Law San Francisco remains focused on providing students the best legal education. The school counts former Vice President Kamala Harris and former San Francisco Mayor and Assembly Speaker Willie Brown among its alumni.

Restorative Justice Alongside the Renaming

Beyond the symbolic name change, AB 1936 specified several restorative justice initiatives, including pro bono legal aid for tribal courts and dedicated scholarships for members of the Round Valley Indian Tribes, according to UC Law SF. The school has also worked to establish an Indigenous Law Center, which is active. School leaders worked directly with tribal leadership on those commitments as the renaming moved through the Legislature.

The resolution of the naming dispute comes as UC Law SF continues reshaping its physical footprint in San Francisco's Civic Center. In bold Tenderloin expansion move, the school agreed in April to house San Francisco State University's graduate business school within its Tenderloin Academic Village at 198 McAllister Street, with San Francisco State University planning to move the programs into the space in July 2026 and classes beginning the following month, continuing years of academic and physical growth in the neighborhood.
news.summary: The U.S. Supreme Court rejected descendants' bid to restore Serranus Hastings' name on San Francisco's 148-year-old law school.

news.title: How Religious Groups Have Changed their Political Allegiances Over the Past Election Cycle
news.text: White Catholic voters continue to favor Republicans heading into the November midterm elections, but their support contrasts sharply with Hispanic Catholics and several other religious groups backing Democratic House candidates.According to a Pew Research Center survey, Republicans lead among White Catholic registered voters by 50% to 32%, while Hispanic Catholics favor Democrats by 59% to 19%. Across Catholics overall, Democrats hold a narrow numerical advantage, 42% to 39%, with another 19% unsure or supporting another candidate.The divisions extend beyond Catholicism as White evangelical Protestants favor Republican House candidates by 73% to 12%. Black Protestants prefer Democrats by 74% to 6%, while religiously unaffiliated voters support Democrats by 61% to 17%. White nonevangelical Protestants divide 45% Republican to 37% Democratic, a difference Pew says is not statistically significant.The survey, conducted September 28 through October 4 among 5,062 adults, including 3,917 registered voters, shows why broad descriptions of Christian or religious voters can obscure substantial differences within those categories.The previous midterms offer a historical comparison. In 2022, White Catholics voted Republican by a 25-percentage-point margin, while Hispanic Catholics favored Democrats by 34 points, according to Pew's validated-voter analysis. The current poll puts those advantages at 18 points and 40 points, respectively.White evangelical Protestants also remain firmly Republican, although their current preferences are less lopsided than their voting in the previous midterms. In 2022, they supported Republican House candidates by 86% to 12%, an overwhelming 74-point margin. Their current Republican advantage is 61 points.Religiously unaffiliated voters, including atheists, agnostics and people describing their religion as "nothing in particular," supported Democrats by 72% to 27% in 2022. Their current Democratic advantage is numerically similar, although neither party reaches its previous vote share because some respondents remain uncommitted.The 2024 presidential election demonstrated that familiar religious alliances can persist while the margins change. Donald Trump won Protestant voters by 62% to 36% and Catholics by 55% to 43%, according to Pew. Catholics had divided almost evenly in 2020, when Joe Biden received 50% and Trump 49%.Among religiously unaffiliated voters, Kamala Harris won 70% to Trump's 28% in 2024, close to Biden's 71% to 26% advantage four years earlier. White evangelical Protestants remained a central Republican constituency, with 81% supporting Trump in 2024, compared with 83% in 2020.Participation helped determine those outcomes. Pew found that Trump's Catholic gains reflected both voters switching candidates and changes in turnout. Seven percent of Catholics who backed Biden in 2020 moved to Trump in 2024, while 4% of Catholic Trump voters switched to Harris.The remaining improvement came from differences in who voted. Religious attendance also divided the electorate in the last midterms. Voters attending services at least monthly favored Republicans by 67% to 31% in 2022. Those attending a few times a year or less preferred Democrats by 56% to 42%.Jewish voters also favor Democrats in separate national polling. A GBAO Strategies survey for the Jewish Voters Resource Center found that 67% planned to support Democratic congressional candidates, compared with 26% backing Republicans.Conducted August 26 through September 1 among 800 self-identified Jewish voters, the survey had a margin of error of 3.5 percentage points. Its 41-point Democratic advantage compares with the 36-point margin Jewish voters gave Democratic House candidates in 2022, according to Pew. Different samples and methods prevent treating that comparison as a precise measure of movement.Among Muslim voters, separate research documents a fractured Democratic coalition in the last presidential election, although it does not provide a comparable 2026 congressional preference. The Institute for Social Policy and Understanding's American Muslim Poll, fielded by NORC in April and May 2025, found that 50% of Muslim voters reported supporting Kamala Harris in 2024, 31% Donald Trump and 12% Green Party candidate Jill Stein.The same survey found that only 55% of Muslims who reported voting for Joe Biden in 2020 backed Harris four years later. Another 10% supported Trump, 16% chose another candidate and 19% did not vote for president.
